records.subject: fix(sairnroofing): the photo rule now bites, ids are server-verified, and unavailable material stops posing as a met threshold
records.summary: sairnroofing's photo requirement did not actually refuse, record ids were minted client-side rather than server-verified, and material that was UNAVAILABLE still counted toward a met threshold -- so a claim could present as fully evidenced on photos that were never required, ids the server never issued, and stock that was not there. rf_claim_photos is Tier A.

records.phase_note: Three related decisions -- a rule that did not bite, client-minted ids, and an unavailable material counting toward a met threshold -- all read as original design rather than drift.

contributing_factors.factor: `evidence_gap` was a STRING ANNOTATION and nothing more. A slope with 40 hits and zero photos still returned meets_threshold with a note beside it, and a carrier does not read the note.
contributing_factors.action: a count reaches meets_threshold ONLY if a photo backs the slope. Unbacked counts are reported in full as insufficient_evidence, with the reason stated -- suppressing them would hide real field work and scoring them would assert evidence the app cannot show.

contributing_factors.factor: Record ids were MINTED CLIENT-SIDE. Cited photo ids came from the payload and were only filtered for blanks, so a claim could cite photographs that do not exist.
contributing_factors.action: cited ids are checked against the real photo rows server-side.

contributing_factors.factor: Material recorded UNAVAILABLE still counted toward a met threshold, so unavailable stock supported a claim.
contributing_factors.action: unavailable material no longer counts toward the threshold.

contributing_factors.factor: A GUARD THAT ANNOTATES RATHER THAN REFUSES LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE ONE THAT ENFORCES, from inside the code and from the panel. The string was present, the field was populated, and every reading of the record showed the concern had been noticed.
contributing_factors.note: The class is wider than this app: a field that records a concern and a branch that acts on one are different things, and nothing sweeps for the first being mistaken for the second. Named rather than closed.

contributing_factors.factor: Found by a BEHAVIOUR-LEVEL COMPARISON OF TWO BUILDS (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-26-repair-vs-replace-two-implementations.md), not by a check. Three defects in one surface surfaced together because a second implementation existed to compare against.

records.recurrence_open: NOT CLOSED FOR THE CLASS. Three specific rules now bite in sairnroofing. records.subject: fix(sairndental): a failed booking left a patient record the practice cannot delete
records.summary: api/sairndental/public-book.js wrote a dnt_patients row before the appointment it exists for, and a failed booking left that patient record behind with no route to remove it -- on an unauthenticated public endpoint, so an anonymous caller could accumulate them. PHI created by a transaction that did not complete, in a practice that cannot delete it.

injection.unknown_reason: The orphan is a consequence of the booking endpoint's ordering, which has been its shape since the endpoint was written; no single commit introduced the missing rollback, so blaming one would be a guess dressed as a fact.

records.citation_note: No standing rule covers 'a partial write on a failure path leaves a record the owner cannot remove'. The nearest is the removal-path work on the SAIRNbiz pair, which is about a MISSING verb rather than about an orphan created by a failed transaction.
records.phase_note: Read from the fix: a patient row is written before the appointment that justifies it, with no compensating delete on the failure path. An ordering decision, not a coding slip.

contributing_factors.factor: The patient row was written BEFORE the appointment it exists for, so every booking that then failed left an orphan. The most common failure is the 409 slot race two people hit on purpose by clicking the same popular time.
contributing_factors.action: the order is reversed -- claim the SLOT first, write the patient only once it is secured, so a 409 or a 502 leaves no trace.

contributing_factors.factor: The patient write was a bare `await fetch(...)` whose result was never checked. On failure patientId still pointed at a row that did not exist and the appointment was written referencing a PHANTOM PATIENT, reported as a clean 200.
contributing_factors.action: the result is checked and the response carries patient_record: 'saved' | 'not_saved'.
contributing_factors.note: This is the same write-path shape as cluster 5b98fd27: a call whose result nobody reads, reported as success.

contributing_factors.factor: CLEANING UP AFTERWARDS WAS NEVER AVAILABLE AS A FIX. dnt_patients has no delete grant -- revoked platform-wide by sql/unused_delete_grant_revoke_2026-08-24.sql -- so the debris is permanent PHI in a dental record system and no remediation path existed.
contributing_factors.note: The revoke is correct and is not being undone. What it means is that any write which can create an orphan is unrecoverable by construction, so the ordering fix is the only available class of fix. Recorded so a future session does not reach for a cleanup that cannot exist.

contributing_factors.factor: The endpoint is PUBLIC AND UNAUTHENTICATED, so anyone able to load the booking page could mint unbounded rows carrying name, date of birth, phone and email just by racing a slot or retrying a failing one. Nothing bounded the rate or the volume.
contributing_factors.note: The ordering fix removes the orphan, not the exposure of an unauthenticated write path to a PHI table. That is a wider question than this defect and is not closed here.

contributing_factors.factor: The open-work row named ONE of the two defects. The phantom-patient write was found only by reading the code while fixing the first, not by the process that recorded it.
contributing_factors.note: Not actioned as a process change here. It is the argument for tools/optimistic_success_scan.py, which looks for exactly this shape -- a dropped write and a success reported anyway -- across the platform rather than one site at a time.

records.recurrence_open: NOT CLOSED FOR THE CLASS. The ordering fix is specific to this endpoint. The unauthenticated PHI write path remains, dnt_patients still has no delete grant so any future orphan is permanent, and the booking is still reported successful when only the patient write fails -- deliberately, because the slot IS taken, but it means a partial failure still reads as a clean booking to the visitor.

contributing_factors.note: This is the quiet-wrong-answer class the Benford and invariant work exists for, and neither covers coverage rules.

records.subject: fix(tests): two suite runs at once made every probe restore the wrong file
records.summary: Concurrent suite runs made every mutating probe restore the OTHER run's mutation: it stripped a production corruption guard from sairnvet.html repeatedly while reporting "restored byte-identical: True"

contributing_factors.factor: EACH PROBE WAS CORRECT ALONE AND THE SET WAS NOT. A probe snapshots the bytes it reads at its own start and restores them in a finally -- right, in isolation. contributing_factors.action: The runs are serialised, so the invariant each probe assumes -- that it is the only writer -- is actually true.

contributing_factors.factor: THE TRIGGER FIRED AUTOMATICALLY AND ASYNCHRONOUSLY. run_all_tests.py --hook ran on every git push, so THREE concurrent runs were alive in one tree within 43 seconds, plus two copies of one probe started in the same second. contributing_factors.action: The --hook trigger is paused, with the conditions for re-enabling it written down rather than left to judgement.

contributing_factors.factor: THE SYMPTOM WAS A FILE REVERTING OVERNIGHT, WHICH LOOKS LIKE ANYTHING BUT THIS. sairnvet.html repeatedly lost the corrupt-store guard, and an exemptions file kept an entry no run had failed to remove -- both read as a bad merge, a stale editor, or somebody else's clone.
contributing_factors.action: The mechanism is written down with the timestamps, because the next occurrence will present the same way and the diagnosis is not reachable from the symptom.

records.recurrence_open: Serialising the runs removes the concurrency this trigger created. It does not make a probe safe to run beside anything else -- two humans, or a human and a cron, still produce the same interleaving, and no probe detects that it is not the only writer.

records.subject: fix(sairngrounds,tools): forty-three writes, no timeout, and a weather message said otherwise
records.summary: 43 server writes with no timeout on any path: a hung fetch never returns from the await, so grdData's catch never runs and the toast naming what failed to sync never fires at all

contributing_factors.factor: A HUNG FETCH NEITHER RESOLVES NOR REJECTS, so the whole well-built failure path never runs. Forty of the 43 writes read `var syncResult = await grdData(...)` and toast exactly what failed to sync -- and against a black-holed connection the await never returns, the catch never fires, and the user clicks Save and the screen says nothing.
contributing_factors.action: AbortSignal.timeout(15000) inside grdData(), feature-detected, landing an AbortError in the catch that already returns null -- one edit rather than a push helper, because this file already had a shared failure vocabulary where null means 'did not reach the server' at all 43 sites.

contributing_factors.factor: THE QUALITY OF THE REFUSAL PATH IS WHAT MADE THE GAP INVISIBLE. An app that reports every failed write looks like an app that handles failure; the one fault it cannot report is the one where nothing comes back at all, and that fault is indistinguishable from a slow save.
contributing_factors.action: Stated at the site. The timeout bounds reads too, declared as intended rather than left incidental.

contributing_factors.factor: THE TOOL THAT SHOULD HAVE FOUND IT SAID THE OPPOSITE. write_path_fault_scan.py printed `timeout? yes` because a signal-shaped probe matched two USER-FACING SENTENCES. The app read as protected in the one report anybody would consult.
contributing_factors.action: Recorded as its own register entry and fixed in the same commit -- the scan runs over comment-stripped code and the column is three-state.

records.recurrence_open: The timeout is fifteen seconds in ONE function in ONE app. Twelve other apps still have no timeout on any write path, and the sweep that measures that is the same tool that reported this app as bounded -- it is corrected, not independent. Nothing yet requires a new write path to declare a bound.

records.subject: fix(nav_panel_check): it reported PASS on two apps whose panel system it could not see
records.summary: nav_panel_check reported RESULT:PASS on two apps whose panel system it could not see -- 32 containers invisible, vouching for what it had not looked at

contributing_factors.factor: THE TOOL COULD NOT SEE THE PANEL SYSTEM AND REPORTED PASS. Two apps use 17 and 15 `id="page-x"` containers with showPage(); the checker recognised neither, counted PANEL_COUNT:0, and called that a pass. Thirty-two real containers invisible, and the answer was the same word a clean app gets.
contributing_factors.action: `page-` containers are recognised, and a zero panel count is no longer spelled the same as a clean one.

contributing_factors.factor: THE FILTER GUARANTEED THE TOOL COULD NEVER REPORT ITS OWN FINDING. Adopting only the `page-` ids something CALLS BY NAME is self-defeating: an unreachable container is BY DEFINITION one nothing calls, so the filter removed exactly the panels the tool exists to find. It made one app pass with 16 of 17 by dropping the unreachable one.
contributing_factors.action: A two-container test decides whether the FILE navigates by `page-` at all; if it does, every `page-` container is in scope regardless of whether anything calls it.

contributing_factors.factor: IT HAD BEEN PROMOTED TO THE REPORT-ONLY REGISTRY THAT MORNING, so it was counted as a PASSING CHECKER over two apps it had never looked at. A registry entry converts silence into evidence, and the silence here was a blind spot.
contributing_factors.action: Found by a human read of an unrelated finding in the same app; the promotion is kept, with the coverage correction.

contributing_factors.factor: THIS IS THE FIFTH CORRECTION TO THE SAME FILE AND THE FIRST IN THE SILENT DIRECTION. The previous four -- hardcoded class, hardcoded id, hardcoded nav-function name, hardcoded element -- were all made after it reported a WORKING app as BROKEN, which somebody investigates. A false PASS is investigated by nobody.
contributing_factors.action: Stated as the class in the commit: the four loud failures trained everyone to expect this tool's errors to arrive as false findings, which is the direction that self-corrects.

records.recurrence_open: The tool now recognises two panel conventions. It has no way to say 'this file has a panel system I do not recognise' as distinct from 'this file has no panels' -- and the first is what happened twice here. A third convention would produce the same PASS.

records.subject: fix(sairndental): a refused vendor write showed success and the next sync erased it
records.summary: A refused vendor write showed a success toast and the next sync silently replaced the edit -- a negotiated discount, so it changes what the practice pays

contributing_factors.factor: THREE CORRECT DECISIONS COMPOSED INTO DATA LOSS. Wholesale replacement is the RIGHT design -- it is what makes a REMOVAL expressible, which a merge cannot do. Server-wins on sync is a real choice. A push helper that logs a refusal to console is a real choice. Together: set a discount, the push fails, the toast says it worked, AND THE NEXT SYNC PUTS THE OLD NUMBER BACK, silently.
contributing_factors.action: The write is confirmed before it is trusted -- the missing half, which changes none of the three decisions.

contributing_factors.factor: THE TOAST WAS UNCONDITIONAL AND THE PUSH WAS NOT AWAITED. `dntPushVendorPricing(rules)` on one line and `toast('... set to 12%')` on the next reads as a sequence and is not one: the message is written before the result exists.
contributing_factors.action: The result is read and the message conditioned on it.

contributing_factors.factor: THE SCHEMA HAS BEEN RUN, so this is live rather than prospective. A defect in a code path nobody reaches is a different severity from one a dental practice hits when it changes a vendor discount.
contributing_factors.action: Stated in the record, because 'is this reachable' is the question that separates this from the same shape elsewhere in the same file.

records.recurrence_open: dntPushOne still reports refusals to console.warn only, so every OTHER caller that does not read its result has this shape. The structural scan finds callers that DROP the promise; it does not find a caller that keeps it and then ignores what it says.

records.subject: fix(dental,grounds,scape): stamping is not storage, and a stamp that fails must not lose the save
records.summary: the _m stamp call sat INSIDE the storage try in st()/scpSt() across dental, grounds and scape, so a stamping failure skipped the write and told the user the browser's storage was full -- a false reason and a lost save

contributing_factors.factor: ONE CATCH ANSWERED FOR TWO UNRELATED THINGS. The stamping helper ran inside the try guarding localStorage.setItem, so anything it threw skipped the write entirely and told the user 'this browser storage is full or unavailable' -- A FALSE REASON FOR A BROWSER WHOSE STORAGE WAS FINE, and a lost save.
contributing_factors.action: Stamping has its own try. The failure is LOGGED, naming the key and the consequence, and the write goes ahead UNSTAMPED -- the designed-safe direction, because a missing _m already means the server wins, which is how every record written before the stamp behaves.

contributing_factors.factor: CENTRALISING THE STAMP WAS THE RIGHT CALL AND IS WHAT CREATED THE COUPLING. Adding it once in st()/scpSt() rather than at 486 save sites is correct; the cost is that the one place it lives is inside somebody else's error boundary, and nothing about the diff shows that.
contributing_factors.action: Recorded as the shape: a helper added centrally inherits the error handling of wherever it lands.

contributing_factors.factor: THE TEST FOUND IT BY BREAKING FOR THE WRONG REASON. The harness builds each wrapper with new Function and injects only the globals it names, so the new helper was an unbound identifier; the ReferenceError landed in the STORAGE catch and every good-path arm failed. In a browser the wrapper was fine.
contributing_factors.action: THE EASY FIX WAS TO INJECT THE HELPER AND MOVE ON. Chasing why the harness could not tell the two causes apart is what surfaced the real defect -- because that is exactly the reason a USER could not tell them apart either.

records.recurrence_open: The two halves are now pinned by arms, in three apps. Nothing prevents the NEXT central helper from being added inside the same try, and the only thing that would catch it is a harness failing confusingly again -- which was luck, not a mechanism.

records.subject: fix(tooling): install_git_hooks --check called a clone protected while its hook had never run
records.summary: install_git_hooks.py --check compared core.hooksPath and nothing else, so it printed OK on a clone whose CRLF pre-push hook git had been skipping silently on every push -- and nothing invoked --check at all

contributing_factors.factor: --check ASKED A WEAKER QUESTION THAN install DID. It compared core.hooksPath and stopped; the install path went on to repair CRLF, run the gate and run the shell wrapper. Two entry points to one guarantee, and only one of them checked the whole thing.
contributing_factors.action: --check now asks everything install asks, and CHECKS WITHOUT REPAIRING -- a report-only checker that rewrote a tracked file or this clone's config would be worse than a weak one, and an arm asserts the CRLF is still there afterwards.

contributing_factors.factor: A CRLF SHEBANG NAMES AN INTERPRETER WHOSE NAME ENDS IN A CARRIAGE RETURN, AND GIT SKIPS THE HOOK SILENTLY. On 2026-09-01 all four clones held a CRLF copy and two had core.hooksPath set -- so --check would have printed OK on a hook that had NEVER ONCE EXECUTED.
contributing_factors.action: The byte check is part of --check, because the failure is invisible from every other angle: the file is present, the config is right, and nothing runs.

contributing_factors.factor: AND NOTHING RAN IT ANYWAY. The inventory classified the tool LIBRARY, so no hook, no suite and no gate ever invoked --check. A verifier nobody calls reports nothing, which is indistinguishable from a verifier reporting no problems.
contributing_factors.action: Registered as a report-only checker with args ['--check'], because a BARE invocation installs -- and installing is the one thing report-only must never do.

contributing_factors.factor: .git/ IS NOT VERSIONED, so hooks are per clone and a fresh clone has none until somebody runs the installer. The protection is opt-in by construction and the pre-push hook is the ONLY thing gating a push made by subprocess -- the Claude Code PreToolUse hook keys on Bash command text, and the claim tool pushes from Python.
contributing_factors.action: Stated in the tool's own header, because the scope of what the hook protects is not derivable from the hook.

records.recurrence_open: --check and install now ask the same questions because somebody made them agree, not because anything holds them together. A fifth clone with no hooks is still only found by running the checker, and a sixth check added to install will not appear in --check by itself.

records.subject: feat(audit): item 35 -- daily checkpoints over closed windows, and the verifier that makes them mean something
records.summary: audit-checkpoint's paging guard vanished with its input: the comparison was total !== null && total !== rows.length, so a response carrying no Content-Range, or 0-0/*, skipped the completeness check entirely and a checkpoint was written over one row of three -- a vacuous checkpoint that verifies cleanly forever, which the file's own header names as the thing it must never produce

contributing_factors.factor: THE GUARD WAS WRITTEN AS `total !== null && total !== rows.length`, so the ABSENCE of the thing it checks disabled it. A response with no Content-Range header, or `0-0/*`, made the first clause false and the completeness check was skipped entirely rather than refused.
contributing_factors.action: The read now REFUSES with WINDOW_INCOMPLETE when it cannot establish the total, rather than treating an unknown total as a satisfied comparison.

contributing_factors.factor: THE FAILURE PRODUCES A CHECKPOINT THAT VERIFIES CLEANLY FOREVER. A digest over the first page of a busy day is stable and reproducible and covers a fraction of the window, so every subsequent verification agrees with it -- the file's own header names that as the one thing it must never produce.
contributing_factors.action: Recorded as the shape in the header rather than only as a fixed line, because the next paged digest on this platform will be written by somebody who reads the header.

contributing_factors.factor: IT WAS FOUND BY INDEPENDENT REVIEW AND NOT BY THE SUITE. The suite drove the guard with a well-formed Content-Range in every arm, which is the shape the API returns in normal operation, so no arm ever presented the input that disarmed it.
contributing_factors.action: api/audit-checkpoint.test.js gained arms that present a MISSING and a `0-0/*` Content-Range, which is the state the original arms could not reach.

records.recurrence_open: THE CLASS IS WIDER THAN THIS GUARD: any check written as `x !== null && <predicate on x>` fails open when x is absent, and nothing on this platform scans for that shape. The bounded 14-window re-verification is also still a bound -- it is reported as `full:false` in every response rather than hidden, but a rewritten checkpoint older than the bound is caught only by the cheap prev_digest link, not by a re-digest.

records.subject: fix(sairnlaw,platform): the advisory lock was doing nothing under REPEATABLE READ -- on attorney trust money, and in two other places
records.summary: law_check_and_insert_disbursement holds an advisory lock while summing the trust balance and then inserting, with nothing requiring READ COMMITTED. pg_advisory_xact_lock serialises ACQUISITION and not the SNAPSHOT, so under REPEATABLE READ two concurrent disbursements against one client each sum a balance from before the other committed, both pass the sufficiency check, and both insert -- an overdrawn IOLTA client trust ledger with the lock held correctly throughout. Not exploitable on the current deployment, which uses the default isolation; one ALTER ROLE statement away, and that statement reads as a hardening change.

records.phase_note: Read from the function body: the lock, the aggregate and the insert are all present and correct; what is absent is the isolation precondition they rest on. A design-time omission, not a coding slip.

contributing_factors.factor: pg_advisory_xact_lock serialises ACQUISITION, not the SNAPSHOT. Under REPEATABLE READ a caller that waited on the lock still reads from before the holder committed, so read-decide-write is not atomic however correctly the lock is used.
contributing_factors.action: a guard requiring READ COMMITTED was added to the function.

contributing_factors.factor: THE CODE CONTAINING THE BUG IS CORRECT. The thing that is wrong is a setting in another file -- one ALTER ROLE away -- and that statement reads as a HARDENING change. There is no defect visible at the site to review.

contributing_factors.note: No mechanism proposed here. Giving the toast channel a precedence rule -- a failure message cannot be replaced by a success message -- is a platform-wide UI change with its own failure modes, and it is a larger decision than this fix.

contributing_factors.factor: write_path_fault_scan.py MATCHES THE DATA WRAPPER BY NAME, so a dropped LOCAL ASYNC HELPER is invisible to it. Every one of these calls a helper rather than the wrapper, which is why the apps reported clean while announcing success for writes that never left the device.
contributing_factors.action: tools/optimistic_success_scan.py, whose rule is STRUCTURAL and uses no word list: a caller that drops a write's promise cannot condition anything on the result, so any later toast in that function is unconditional BY CONSTRUCTION. records.recurrence_open: The structural scan finds callers that DROP a write's promise. This caller did not drop anything -- it added a message -- so the scan that found its three siblings could not have found this one, and it was caught by reading the same file. Nothing looks for a second toast raised over a helper that already reported.

records.subject: fix(cron): the watchdog stopped responding to itself and went on grading itself
records.summary: api/cron-watchdog.js wrote its own heartbeat outcome from a report that included its own previous row: partial -> PARTIAL -> partial, so the watchdog's self status could never return to ok once it left it. Latched live; survived the SAIRN_OPS_EMAIL fix landing at 00:15:28Z 2026-09-17. ok in the response body could never be true again, so cron_liveness_check.py could never exit 0.

injection.subject: feat(cron): item 54 -- something now notices when a scheduled job goes silent

records.citation_note: 1.1 is written about a check that CANNOT FAIL; this is the mirror shape -- a check that can never PASS. Same disease: the verdict stopped being a function of the world. Cited rather than not-citable because the mechanism named in 1.1 is exactly what was missing -- nothing made this expression fail on purpose, because no arm could reach it at all.

contributing_factors.factor: the outcome written for this job each run was `bad.length ? 'partial' : 'ok'`, and `bad` is the report INCLUDING this job's own previous row -- so the verdict was a function of the previous verdict, with no input from the world
contributing_factors.action: selfOutcome() removes the self term from the outcome only; the self row is still reported, logged and in not_ok

contributing_factors.factor: the self-exclusion added at 5d0f4459 was applied to the RESPONSE (planResponse takes selfJob) and not to the VERDICT, because it was written from four hours of logs of a LOUD symptom -- HTTP 508 and an hourly alert storm -- and the quiet half had no symptom to reason from
contributing_factors.action: selfOutcome takes the same selfJob from the same SELF_JOB constant, so one spelling covers both halves

contributing_factors.factor: the expression lived inline in the request handler, which no arm drives; 71 arms covered assess() and planResponse() and none could reach it, so the latch was only ever visible in five consecutive production runs
contributing_factors.action: extracted pure and exported; 10 arms incl. a five-run end-to-end drive through assess()+selfOutcome() and a teeth arm running the OLD expression on the same fixture

contributing_factors.factor: a monitor latched red produces no alert and no error -- PARTIAL under an HTTP 200 reads as a run that happened -- and the out-of-band reader that would have caught a watchdog that can never be ok (cron_liveness_check.py via .github/workflows/cron-liveness.yml) has never run: CRON_SECRET is not in the repository Actions secrets and docs/CRON-LIVENESS-STATUS.md still reads COULD NOT TELL as of 2026-09-14
contributing_factors.action: add CRON_SECRET to the repository Actions secrets -- needs Michael; the workflow exists and does nothing until then

AND the fix is verified in the repository only -- the behavioural half lands at the next :15 firing after deploy and has not been observed; the row heals in one run, not instantly.

records.subject: fix(register-gate): a STALE record is told apart from a MISSING one
records.summary: tools/register_feed_gate.py refused with 'no register record cites it' for a commit whose record EXISTED and whose sha a rebase had moved. True about the sha, false about the work, and it sent the reader at --add -- which would write a SECOND record for one defect -- instead of at --reseat, which has always existed for exactly this and is documented on line 5 of defect_register.py's own usage block. Measured cost of the missing pointer: FOUR hand-rolled repairs in one evening, three by CC and at least one by another session, one of which used its own json.dumps and came within a commit of reformatting 5,717 lines of a register whose merge policy is union-by-identity across four clones.

injection.unknown_reason: The wording is how the gate was written rather than something a commit introduced, so naming the commit that created it would record a lag that never elapsed.

records.citation_note: 1.5 is the confident line printed after an error. This is its close relative: a CORRECT refusal whose explanation names the wrong cause, which sends the reader somewhere that makes things worse rather than somewhere that helps. Recorded as arguable because nothing here was reported as a pass.

contributing_factors.factor: The refusal said 'no register record cites it', which is true about the SHA and false about the work -- the record existed and its sha had been moved by a rebase
contributing_factors.action: The refusal now matches the commit's SUBJECT against the register and, when it finds one, says the record EXISTS, names the stale sha, and points at --reseat

contributing_factors.factor: --reseat has always existed and is documented on line 5 of defect_register.py's own usage block, so the capability was never missing -- only a pointer at the moment somebody needs it
contributing_factors.action: The pointer is now printed at the refusal, which is the only moment the reader is looking

contributing_factors.factor: A rebase between recording and pushing is the ORDINARY case on a four-clone night, not an exception, so this refusal is hit routinely and its wording is read under time pressure
contributing_factors.note: Nothing can stop another session pushing between a rebase and a push. What can change is what the refusal says when it happens, which is what changed.

contributing_factors.factor: Four hand-rolled repairs in one evening and none of the four authors reached for the documented command -- the failure is discoverability, and one of the repairs used its own JSON writer and came within a commit of reformatting 5,717 lines of a union-by-identity register
contributing_factors.action: Probe section H holds the pointer in BOTH directions, so a refusal that stops distinguishing stale from missing goes red rather than quietly reverting to the old wording

records.recurrence_open: The pointer fires on SUBJECT equality, so a rebase that also REWORDS the commit still reads as missing rather than stale -- and an --amend that changes the message is exactly that case. Nothing here detects it, and the reader would again be told to --add. Stated rather than left to be found the fifth time.

records.subject: fix(dispatch): the claim panel read the working tree and ignored the expiry
records.summary: tools/dispatch_state.py's ACTIVE CLAIMS panel -- the thing a session reads before starting work -- read .claude/claims from the WORKING TREE and treated any status=='active' entry as live. sairn_claim.py, which owns the claim record, reads origin/main (a claim another session pushed is only a fact once it is there) and applies the 4-hour expiry. Measured 2026-09-16: dispatch_state listed a 74.4-hour-old fourth claim as ACTIVE while sairn_claim.py list did not show it at all. Both differences run in the LOOSE direction, so the panel always looked more informative than the authority. Fixed by calling load_all(from_origin=True) and is_active() rather than by growing a second reader.

injection.unknown_reason: live_claims() was written with a local read from the start, so there is no commit that introduced the divergence -- it is the shape the function was born with. Naming the commit that added the function would record an injection lag that never elapsed.

records.citation_note: 2.3 is a fact with a tense needing a read and a number needing a SINGLE SOURCE. The single-source half is exact here -- one claim record, two readers, two answers. The rule's worked examples are about standing documents rather than about two tools, so it is recorded as arguable.

contributing_factors.factor: live_claims() re-implemented a read that sairn_claim.py already owned, instead of calling it -- two readers of one record, free to disagree
contributing_factors.action: dispatch_state now calls sairn_claim.load_all(from_origin=True) and sairn_claim.is_active(), and the dormant import subprocess it would have needed is gone

contributing_factors.factor: Both differences run in the LOOSE direction -- a local read shows more claims than origin does, and no expiry shows more than the 4-hour rule does -- so the tool always looked more informative than the authority, never less
contributing_factors.note: A panel that lists MORE active claims reads as more thorough. Nothing about the output invites the question of whether the extra rows are real, which is why a 74-hour-old claim sat in it unremarked.

records.subject: test(G5): the employees read -- and `hourly_rate` was in NO test on the platform
records.summary: api/sd-data-employees-refusal.test.js asserted nothing about the manager payroll strip: deleting `if (session.role !== 'owner') { delete copy.hourly_rate; }` from api/sd-data.js left the suite GREEN, and `hourly_rate` appeared in NO test anywhere on the platform. injection.unknown_reason: The strip and the suite were written at different times and no commit shows an arm for it being removed, so there is no injection point to cite -- the assertion was never there. Recorded as unknown rather than attributed to whichever commit added the strip.

records.citation_note: 1.1 is a check that cannot fail. Here the check did not EXIST, and the suite around it was strong enough that its absence read as coverage. Cited because the end state is the same and because the probe that found it is 1.1's own prescribed mechanism.

contributing_factors.factor: THE PROMISE LIVED IN A COMMENT. 'Manager: full roster visibility, but never payroll' is a sentence in the source, and the code implementing it was correct -- so every reader who checked was reassured, and nothing mechanical ever asked.
contributing_factors.action: Three arms: a manager gets no hourly_rate and KEEPS title, an owner still gets hourly_rate, and the stored row is not mutated.

contributing_factors.factor: IT IS A SECOND GUARANTEE LIVING INSIDE THE FIRST ONE'S BRANCH. The role deny-list decides WHO reads the roster; the strip decides WHAT they see. A suite organised around the first question has no natural place to ask the second, and the arms that do exist assert on a fixture row carrying no payroll field at all -- so they could not have reached it.
contributing_factors.action: The new arms use a fixture row that DOES carry hourly_rate, which is the change that makes the question askable.

contributing_factors.factor: ONE ARM WOULD HAVE BEEN WEAKER THAN IT LOOKED. 'The manager sees no hourly_rate' is satisfied by an empty response, by a refusal, and by a strip that removed everything -- so it is paired with an OWNER arm that requires the field to still be there, and with a title assertion, because full visibility is the other half of the same sentence.
contributing_factors.action: Three arms rather than one, each named for what it rules out.

contributing_factors.factor: THE STRIP MUTATES A COPY FOR A REASON THE SOURCE STATES AND NOTHING CHECKED: a delete on the upstream object would remove payroll from whatever the client library cached, so the next OWNER read would be missing it too. A correctness property of the fix that fails silently and in the opposite direction from the one being guarded.
contributing_factors.action: Driven: the fixture row is inspected after a manager read.

records.recurrence_open: The three arms cover ONE field on ONE resource. Nothing enumerates which other fields are stripped by role anywhere on the platform, and a strip is invisible to every check that asserts on a fixture row not carrying the field -- which is how this one survived. records.subject: fix(grounds,scape): a vanished write also vanished from the console in two of three apps
records.summary: sairngrounds and sairnscape reported a refused localStorage write to the USER and to nothing else: their storage catch toasted and logged nothing, so a write that vanished also vanished from the console and a support read of a browser log showed no trace. sairndental's copy of the same wrapper carries a console.error with the reason written beside it -- the line was added to one of three near-identical files when the stamping catch was split out on 2026-09-13

records.citation_note: No section covers a fix landing in one of several near-identical files. It is adjacent to the byte-identical-is-not-safe-in-context discipline, but that one is about propagating a pattern TO a new context; this is about failing to propagate it at all.

contributing_factors.factor: ONE FIX APPLIED TO ONE OF THREE FILES. The stamping catch was split out of the storage catch in all three apps on 2026-09-13, and the console line that makes the STORAGE failure reportable was added in sairndental only. contributing_factors.factor: A TOAST IS NOT A LOG AND THEY FAIL IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS. The toast reaches the person in front of the screen and is gone in eight seconds; the console reaches whoever reads the browser log afterwards, which is the only channel a support read has. Having one is indistinguishable from having both at the moment of the failure.
contributing_factors.action: Stated in the code at both sites, quoting the sentence sairndental already carried.

contributing_factors.factor: The reader was built against svData's BEHAVIOUR as its author understood it, not against api/sd-data.js. The server comment saying why the flag exists was never read from the client side.
contributing_factors.action: section C0 of the suite drives the REAL svData against a fake fetch and pins the contract in both modes, so the client and server halves can no longer disagree silently.

contributing_factors.factor: An unprovisioned table and an empty table are indistinguishable at the HTTP layer by design -- both are 200 with an empty array -- so every consumer of this transport is one dropped field away from the same false statement.
contributing_factors.action: the other 40 sv_* resources have not been audited for the same assumption; svHydrateAll carries a comment asserting the same wrong belief and survives only because it early-returns on an empty array.

records.summary: reverifySubscription() and reverifyTrial() fell back to the client-only check whenever the verify request THREW, with no time bound -- so blocking the request (offline, a hosts entry, DevTools) made a stored, forgeable localStorage record grant access INDEFINITELY, with nothing ever re-asked. records.citation_note: No section covers a correct fallback with no bound on it. It is the inverse of the fail-closed rule -- this one fails OPEN deliberately, which is right for a cost/availability trade and wrong without a ceiling -- and inventing a citation would blur the rule that does exist.

contributing_factors.factor: THE FALLBACK IS CORRECT AND HAD NO BOUND, which are two different facts that read as one. A paying customer with no network must not lose the app, so falling back to the last known answer is right; nothing said for how long, so the answer was reused forever.
contributing_factors.action: A 72-hour grace measured from the last real server answer, stamped in saveSub/saveTrial rather than at the four call sites so a new call site cannot forget it.

contributing_factors.factor: THE FAILURE IS REACHED BY DOING NOTHING. contributing_factors.action: Recorded as the shape. The bound is the only client-side answer: the decision cannot be made better, only reused for less long.

contributing_factors.factor: A FUTURE TIMESTAMP WOULD HAVE REINTRODUCED THE UNBOUNDED WINDOW THROUGH THE FIELD THAT BOUNDS IT. `age <= GRACE` is satisfied by any negative age, so clock skew or a stamp written ahead restores exactly what was removed.
contributing_factors.action: `age >= 0` guards it, and a mutation removing that guard is driven by the probe.

contributing_factors.factor: AN EXISTING ARM STOPPED REACHING ITS SUBJECT WHEN THE BOUND WAS ADDED. contributing_factors.action: Its fixture carries a fresh stamp, so it tests the expiry guard rather than re-testing the bound. A guard added upstream can make a downstream arm vacuous without either being wrong.

records.recurrence_open: THE BOUND IS NOT AUTHENTICATION AND THE RESIDUAL IS OPEN: localStorage is attacker-controlled, so a forger who knows the field writes lastVerifiedAt and buys another 72 hours. records.subject: fix(tier-a-gate): an obligation can be recorded for work already pushed, because one had to be
records.summary: tools/tier_a_review_gate.py is satisfied PER RESOURCE, not per change. Commit 7005253c -- a real product change adding a server-side role check on the sb_po/sb_recv void transition in api/sd-data.js -- pushed UNBLOCKED because an obligation for those two resources was already open from a test-only change earlier the same day, whose own recorded text reads 'NEW NEGATIVE CONTROL, no product code changed'. So an authorization change to a Tier A money path was recorded by nobody, and the entry a reviewer would read describes something else. Found by noticing the gate did NOT fire on my own push when the diff plainly names both resources.

injection.unknown_reason: The per-resource semantics is how the gate was built, not something a commit introduced, so there is no injection sha to name. Pointing at the commit that created the tool would record a lag that never elapsed.

records.citation_note: 1.1 is a check that stopped checking. This one never stopped: it answers a narrower question than its own refusal text implies -- 'a Tier A change is reviewed by a session OTHER than the one that wrote it' reads as a claim about the CHANGE, and the mechanism is about the RESOURCE. Same end state, different route, so the citation is arguable.

contributing_factors.factor: The gate answers 'is there an OPEN obligation for this resource' rather than 'is THIS CHANGE recorded', so any open entry satisfies any later change touching the same resource
contributing_factors.action: Per-change obligations are the real fix and are NOT made in this commit -- changing what a blocking gate refuses is a separate act from being able to record the truth about a change it let through. Recorded here so the decision is visible rather than assumed.

contributing_factors.factor: Obligations accumulate faster than they are discharged, so on an active resource there is nearly always one open -- which means the gate is silently permissive on exactly the resources being worked hardest
contributing_factors.note: This is a property of the queue, not of the code. It gets better only when discharges keep pace with opens, which is a staffing fact rather than a change.

contributing_factors.factor: cmd_open() read the working diff plus the UNPUSHED range, and both are empty by the time anybody notices the gate let something through -- so there was no way to record an accurate obligation after the fact
contributing_factors.action: --open ... --range A..B, refusing a malformed range and refusing an empty one with the distinction stated

contributing_factors.factor: Nothing compares an obligation's TEXT to the change that satisfied it. The entry that covered a server-side authorization change says in its own words 'no product code changed', and no mechanism reads that sentence
contributing_factors.note: Comparing recorded prose to a diff is a judgement, not a check, and a tool that guessed would either nag on every honest entry or pass on every dishonest one. The per-change fix above removes the need for it.

records.recurrence_open: THE DEFECT ITSELF IS STILL OPEN. What this commit fixes is only the repair path -- an accurate obligation can now be recorded for work already pushed, and one was. Every future change touching a resource with an open obligation will still pass unrecorded, and nobody is told. The count of changes that have already ridden in this way is not known and is not derivable from the register, because the register only holds what somebody opened.

records.subject: fix(auth): a deactivated employee kept read and write on every gated resource -- the 2026-08-23 fix was app-shaped and the defect was not
records.summary: api/sd-data.js verified a session token's signature and expiry and never re-checked whether the credential behind it was still active, so a DEACTIVATED employee kept gated read and write access to thirteen apps' resources for the remaining life of a 12h token. 9fef0f35 closed this for api/sc-auth.js's own roster and set_active on 2026-08-23; the data path was never covered. CRITICAL under the defined vocabulary: after deactivation the caller is unauthorised, the access reaches real tenant data, and it was reachable on the real deployment by a real caller rather than in principle

injection.unknown_reason: api/sd-data.js gated on the token claim from its first version; there is no commit where a current-state re-check was removed

records.citation_note: no standing rule names 'an authorisation claim inside a still-valid token outliving the state it asserts'; the rules are about checks and writes, and stretching 1.11 to cover an auth-lifetime shape would blur it

contributing_factors.factor: THE PREVIOUS FIX WAS APP-SHAPED AND THE DEFECT WAS NOT. 9fef0f35 closed the deactivated-credential gap for api/sc-auth.js's own roster and set_active, and api/_lib/employee-lifecycle.js carried the same re-check for the apps that share it. The DATA path shared neither, so a fix that read as a class fix left thirteen apps' gated resources open for another three weeks.
contributing_factors.action: credentialStillActive() lives in api/_lib/auth.js, beside the thing that MINTS the token, and is awaited at the sd-data session gate immediately after verifySessionToken and before any resource handler -- one place both paths reach rather than a second copy of the rule.

contributing_factors.factor: A SIGNED TOKEN CARRIES ROLE AS A CLAIM. Verifying it proves the claim was minted and says nothing about whether it is still true, and nothing in the gate distinguished those two questions -- so 'the session is valid' silently meant 'the employee is still employed'.
contributing_factors.action: The sabotage arm signs ONE token, verifies it, flips the row behind it, and requires the same byte-identical token to be refused 403 CREDENTIAL_INACTIVE -- which is the only form of proof that separates the two questions.

contributing_factors.factor: NOTHING OBSERVABLE DISTINGUISHED THE TWO STATES. Every request from a deactivated employee succeeded, raised no error and wrote no log, and the window closed on its own when the token expired up to twelve hours later. There was no failing request for anyone to notice, and deactivation is the one control an owner has for somebody who has just left.
contributing_factors.action: api/sd-data-active-credential.test.js holds that sd-data calls it, AWAITS it, in the right ORDER, refuses only on CREDENTIAL_INACTIVE, and cannot be broken by its own logging.

contributing_factors.factor: THE APP-TO-TABLE MAP HAS NO RULE. Fifteen apps: sd, sb, grd and scp use a prefix, the rest the full app name, and sairncare's table is not alf_* though its endpoint is. A derived map would have been wrong for at least five apps and wrong SILENTLY, because a missing table reads as 'no active row' and would refuse every caller in that app.
contributing_factors.action: The map is DECLARED, never derived, and stonedesk_sub is deliberately absent with NO_ACTIVE_CHECK as its answer because subcontractors key on sub_id.

records.recurrence_open: THE THIRD STATE LETS THE REQUEST THROUGH ON PURPOSE. NO_ACTIVE_CHECK continues when the app has no employee table or the lookup itself fails, because a transport failure is not a deactivation and refusing every user whenever the database blinks is the worse failure. That trade is right and it means a sustained database fault RE-OPENS this gap for as long as it lasts; only the log makes it visible and nothing alarms on a run of them. The declared table map is hand-kept for the same good reason, so a sixteenth app added without an entry answers NO_ACTIVE_CHECK and is unprotected, silently.

records.subject: fix(tests): two arms of mine were about my habits, not the register's rules

injection.unknown_reason: The arms were introduced with the probe itself on 2026-09-15 and were wrong from the first line, so the injection commit is the commit that added the file -- naming it as a regression point would misdescribe an original-design defect.

records.citation_note: No standing rule names 'a control encoding its author's style as a requirement'. The nearest is the platform's refusal of word lists, which is stated in tool headers rather than in the process rules, so citing a section would be inventing one.
records.phase_note: Both arms were written correct-looking against the only records that existed at the time, which were the author's own.

contributing_factors.factor: An arm required the LITERAL string 'NOT CLOSED' in recurrence_open, which is how its author happens to write them. Another session stated the residual in its own words and the probe failed a correct record.
contributing_factors.action: the arm now asserts the PROPERTY -- states a residual, does not dismiss one -- rather than a wording.

contributing_factors.factor: A CONTROL WRITTEN BY ONE AUTHOR AGAINST A SHARED ARTEFACT ENCODES THAT AUTHOR'S HABITS AS RULES. Both arms passed for days because only their author's records existed to test them against; they failed the first time somebody else wrote one.

records.recurrence_open: NOT CLOSED FOR THE CLASS. records.subject: feat(tools): a sweep for the class -- and it found a second instance on its first run
records.summary: api/sairndental/public-book.test.js asserted `reached || res.statusCode !== 400 || res.body.error.code !== 'NOTES_TOO_LONG'` for an arm titled "passes validation and REACHES THE NETWORK STAGE". Any one term satisfied it, and the request was 502ing before it reached anything -- because the block's resolveSlug stub throws unconditionally and public-book.js destructures it at module load, so NO arm in that block could ever get past validation. The arm was green the whole time

injection.unknown_reason: The arm and its harness stub appear to have arrived together, and no commit in the file's history shows the disjunction being ADDED to a previously-strict assertion. Recorded as unknown rather than attributed to the file's creation commit on a guess.

records.citation_note: The arm could fail, and could not fail for the state it described. Same end state as 1.1 -- an assertion that cannot go red when its claim stops being true -- reached through a disjunction rather than through decay.

contributing_factors.factor: THE ASSERTION WAS A THREE-WAY DISJUNCTION, SO ANY ONE TERM SATISFIED IT. `reached || res.statusCode !== 400 || res.body.error.code !== 'NOTES_TOO_LONG'` is green whenever the handler dies early, refuses with a 500, or refuses with a 400 carrying any other code. The arm already recorded its own claim exactly, in `reached`; the other two terms could only weaken it.
contributing_factors.action: Reduced to `assert.ok(reached, ...)`, with the observed status and error code interpolated into the failure message so the next reader gets the diagnosis rather than a bare false.

contributing_factors.factor: THE HARNESS MADE THE ARM IMPOSSIBLE TO PASS HONESTLY, WHICH IS WHY THE WEAK PREDICATE WAS LOAD-BEARING. public-book.js DESTRUCTURES resolveSlug at module load, and the block's stub throws unconditionally, so no arm in it could get past validation -- including the one whose entire subject is getting past validation. The disjunction was what let it look like it had.
contributing_factors.action: The stub is switchable and exactly one arm turns it on; every validation arm keeps the refusal it relies on.

contributing_factors.factor: IT WAS FOUND BY A SWEEP BUILT FOR A DIFFERENT FILE, ON ITS FIRST RUN, over 330 suites. Nothing about this suite was suspected -- it was green, in an app with no open findings, and the title read correctly.
contributing_factors.action: tools/negated_status_assertion_scan.py, registered report-only in PURPOSES. Deliberately a READ-LIST: `!== <code>` is correct when the claim is that some OTHER lock answered, and no mechanical rule separates that from 'it got through'.

contributing_factors.factor: A GREEN ARM WITH A TRUE-SOUNDING TITLE IS THE HARDEST KIND TO DOUBT. 'passes validation and reaches the network stage' is exactly what a reader wants to be true, and the only thing contradicting it was a status code nobody printed.
contributing_factors.action: The failure message prints the status and the error code, so the arm cannot fail without saying which stage it stopped at.

It does NOT find `assert.notStrictEqual(code, 401)`, which is the same claim with no literal operator, and it cannot see a disjunction whose weak term is not a status comparison at all -- `reached || somethingElse` would be invisible. It found this one because one term happened to carry the shape it scans for.

records.subject: fix(csv): a customer name beginning with = executed as a formula in whoever opened the export -- 53 places, 13 files, one copy-pasted line
records.summary: Every CSV export on the platform wrote cells as quote + String(c).replace(/quote/g, double) + quote -- correct RFC 4180 quoting and no defence against formula injection. Excel, LibreOffice and Google Sheets execute a cell beginning =, +, - or @ as a formula on open, and the surrounding quotes do not prevent it because the importer strips them as syntax before evaluating. Any user-typed field (customer name, memo, complaint body) was executable content in the recipient spreadsheet, with =cmd reaching DDE and =IMPORTXML exfiltrating the adjacent row. 53 sites across 13 files, one line copied repeatedly; stonedesk.html held 39 of them in 36 script blocks. Four apps were worse than the rest: their quoter was CONDITIONAL and emitted the cell entirely unquoted when it contained no comma, quote or newline, including api/_lib/roofing-gl-export.js whose memo field ships to an accountant for import.

injection.unknown_reason: The line predates any commit that could be called its origin -- it appears in the earliest versions of several apps and was copied between them, so naming one sha would pick an arbitrary member of a family.

records.citation_note: No standing rule in SAIRN-PROCESS-RULES.md covers output encoding for a downstream interpreter; the rules there are about checks, indexes, pushes and claims. Inventing a citation would be worse than saying so.
records.phase_note: The expression is correct RFC 4180 quoting written by somebody solving the comma problem, then copied 53 times. Nothing about the design was wrong; the line simply never considered the importer as an interpreter.

records.subject: fix(dental): the CDT catalogue was versioned and the charges were not -- a posted charge re-read whatever the catalogue said today

records.subject: fix(hydration): a full store silently switched server-wins OFF for good -- in all seven apps, because the flag write's return was discarded one line below a map write whose return is read
records.summary: SyncedBootstrap() in all SEVEN server-wins apps read st()'s return for the synced-map write -- with a comment saying 'the flag must NOT outlive a failed map write' -- and DISCARDED it for the bootstrap-flag write one line below. Driven in a harness taught to refuse a write: on a full store the map lands, the flag does not, BootstrappedNow is set, and because the flag is what says the bootstrap has happened, every later load bootstraps again and suppresses overwriting again. ServerWinsMerge()'s overwrite branch is skipped every time, so the device never takes a single correction from the server for the life of the profile -- the defect the whole feature exists to fix, reappearing as its own failure mode, on a device whose only symptom is that nothing ever updates. Fixed by making the two writes atomic: prevRaw captured raw and before the map write, restored exactly on a failed flag write, with removeItem rather than an empty object for the absent case because {} parses and reads as 'seeded nothing'. If the undo also fails the load goes inert and returns 'stuck' rather than 'ran'.

records.summary: sairnlaw.html lawSetClearance() reported Marked cleared over a write the database never performed, for every DISBURSEMENT. api/sd-data.js routes a non-voided Disbursement write to rpc/law_check_and_insert_disbursement; that RPC takes nine named parameters, none of them a clearance field, builds data with jsonb_build_object over ten fixed keys, and on an existing id takes its retry-idempotency branch and returns the stored row HAVING WRITTEN NOTHING. An uncleared CHEQUE is a Disbursement -- the commonest outstanding item in a trust reconciliation and the exact case the 2026-09-18 outstanding-item work was built for -- while DEPOSITS take the plain upsert and store the same field, so the feature appeared to work. With hydration now server-wins the local optimistic copy is erased at the next load, so the firm loses the record and the bank leg silently returns to disagreeing on correct books. Driven against the real handler before the change: the request carries no clearance parameter, and the caller is told it was saved. Fixed as a REFUSAL rather than a store -- the handler compares asked-for against came-back and answers 409 CLEARANCE_NOT_STORED -- which also retires itself if the RPC is ever taught to carry the fields. Making a cheque clearable needs an RPC signature change and a migration and is recorded as open.

records.subject: fix(sairncare,sairnbuild): two check-then-write races closed in Postgres -- a medication record that could be overwritten, and a retainage release that could be lost
records.summary: bld_draws retainage release lost update: the branch read the draw's jsonb data, computed a new retainage_released and appended one audit entry to retainage_release_log client-side, then PATCHed the whole blob back with only license_hash and draw_id in the WHERE clause -- no version or CAS predicate. Two concurrent release_retainage calls on the same draw each read the same starting value and whichever PATCH landed second silently won, discarding the first release's figure AND its audit-trail entry with no error. Fixed by routing through public.bld_release_retainage_atomic(), an optimistic-CAS RPC that compares the row's current retainage_released against what the caller read under pg_advisory_xact_lock and raises RETAINAGE_RELEASE_CONFLICT rather than overwriting blind.

records.subject: fix(sairnlaw): the hours were billed here and the server never heard -- invoiced:true went to localStorage and stopped
records.summary: sairnlaw.html saveInvoice() marked every time entry on a new invoice invoiced=true and wrote the list back with st('law_timeentries', teList) -- localStorage -- while making exactly ONE network write, the invoice itself. The flag that says these hours have been billed never reached the server, so its copy of every billed row still read invoiced:false. Because lawHydrateAll() merges additively and never overwrites a locally-held id, a workstation with no copy yet hydrates those hours FRESH as unbilled, rInvoiceEntryPicker() filters on billable && !invoiced and offers them again, and nothing says they were already sent to the client: the same hours can be invoiced twice. Fixed by writing each touched entry back whole (sd-data.js upserts data:payload wholesale, so a patch would lose hours, rate and billing_code) and by NAMING a write that did not land -- a legacy row with no billing_code is refused by api/_lib/law-timeentry.js, so this can genuinely fail on real data. NOT closed: a device that already holds the entries keeps its stale invoiced:false.

records.subject: fix(tests): the UNGUARDED-overwrite detector was a regex that could NEVER match
records.summary: tests/server_wins_hydration.js's UNGUARDED-overwrite detector shipped as a regex that could NEVER match. The backreference `` -- which is what makes the pattern mean 'the RHS is the same variable whose .id is the key', i.e. an overwrite rather than a seen-set -- was authored through a shell heredoc that consumed the backslash and left a raw 0x01 control byte. The pattern read `= <control-byte>`, matched nothing, and the arm asserting that NOBODY hydrates with an unguarded overwrite passed on every file vacuously. That arm exists because sairnsenior was found shipping four hydrates in exactly that state, invisible to the additive detector; a vacuous version of it reports the whole platform clean. Caught by the push gate's control-byte check, which is precisely the failure mode its own message describes. Fixed by building the pattern with explicit escapes and giving it a two-direction fixture.
