records.phase_note: Coding: d538f1e8 fixed the declaration-as-own-evidence defect for TABLED files and did not carry it into the untabled branch. Inferred rather than stated -- nothing in that commit records a decision to leave the other branch alone, so it reads as reach rather than intent.

contributing_factors.factor: The hits loop credits a resource when its name appears anywhere in the body, and the CROSS-TENANT-ISOLATION declaration line is part of the body -- so for an untabled file the declaration satisfied the only evidence test that remained after the WEAK downgrade. A name with nothing else in the file still earns WEAK.
contributing_factors.action: unbacked_declarations() strips the declaration block, including its wrapped continuation lines, and REPORTS every declared name the file does not mention outside it.

contributing_factors.factor: Reporting rather than re-grading is a deliberate limit, not a partial fix: a fourth outcome would reach rank()'s {'GENUINE':0,'WEAK':2,'NONE':3} lookup, which has no key for a new string, and would take the tool down on the first file to hit this branch.
contributing_factors.note: The grade vocabulary is closed by rank(). Widening it is a larger change than this residue justifies, and an arm now reads the grade set from the scanner's own source so a fourth one cannot be added unnoticed.

contributing_factors.factor: Two sessions were handed the same item and fixed the same branch within the hour, with different designs. The collision surfaced as a rebase conflict rather than as a coordination signal, and only because both of us edited the same lines -- a differently-shaped pair of fixes would have merged cleanly and left two rules fighting.
contributing_factors.action: Declared in the status registry to the other session before starting, with an explicit offer to hand it back; the conflict was then resolved to their design rather than mine, and this record says which parts of each survived.

records.recurrence_open: The residue is REPORTED, not re-graded: a declared name with nothing behind it still earns WEAK, and only a reader of UNDECLARED will see that it rests on nothing. Closing it properly needs rank() to carry a fourth outcome, which is a larger change than this justifies today. And the whole branch remains ARMED AND UNEXERCISED -- 683 test files, 5 declarations, all three that declare resources are tabled -- so neither the downgrade nor this report has ever fired on real data, and both rest entirely on synthetic fixtures.

records.subject: fix(sairncare): the trail's "On" column showed a date, and the refusal it serves promises the reader can tell which one is later
records.summary: prRenderRecorded() in sairncare.html rendered the alf_claim_routes trail's 'On' column as String(created_at).slice(0,10) -- DATE ONLY. The 409 ALREADY_RECORDED that this trail exists to serve tells the biller: 'record it again and the trail will show both, with the later one as what is believed now.' Two determinations recorded the same day carried IDENTICAL text, so the reader could not tell which was later EVEN WITH BOTH IN FRONT OF THEM -- the app made a promise in a refusal message that its own display could not keep. Paired with the unordered read in the same trail (b58fb38b/f9e9628f); either alone left the promise half-true, which is why the open-work row required both halves. Fixed by a new fstamp() that parses the timestamptz and renders in the READER'S LOCAL ZONE: slicing the raw ISO string to 16 characters would have been a one-character diff and would print an unmarked UTC clock face, which is worse than a date alone because it looks local and is not.

injection.subject: feat(sairncare): the billing determination is recorded now -- and two of the four "unreachable" resources turned out to have real answers

records.citation_note: No section of docs/SAIRN-PROCESS-RULES.md covers a UI that renders a value at lower precision than the guarantee its own error message makes. The nearest neighbours are about checks that stopped checking, not about a display that never had the precision it promised. Recorded as not-citable rather than stretched onto 1.1, which would put a false citation in the corpus the rule-coverage figures are computed from.

contributing_factors.factor: The trail column was written with the same date-only slice used elsewhere in the file for DATE fields a person typed, without distinguishing those from a timestamptz the server stamped. Same-looking helpers, different sources, different obligations.
contributing_factors.action: New fstamp() alongside fdate(), with a header stating the distinction: fdate takes a typed date string and is RIGHT to show only a date; fstamp takes a server timestamp on an append-only trail and must carry its time.

contributing_factors.factor: The refusal message and the renderer that serves it are in two different files (api/sd-data.js and sairncare.html) and nothing connected the promise to the display. The promise was added later than the display and nobody re-read the display against it.
contributing_factors.action: tests/sairncare_route_record.js now drives BOTH -- the same suite asserts the 409 names the correction path and that the rendered On column carries a time, so the promise and the thing that keeps it fail together.

contributing_factors.factor: The existing suite already drove the real prRenderRecorded and was fully green, because every assertion it made was about content (row present, resident resolved, outcome labelled) and none about precision. Nothing errors when a timestamp is truncated.
contributing_factors.action: A time-carrying arm plus mutation 11 in tests/run_sairncare_route_record_sabotage_probe.py, which restores the date-only slice and is refused. Worth noting what mutation 11 does NOT break: nothing errors and every other arm still passes, which is why the assertion had to be written for it specifically.

contributing_factors.factor: fstamp renders in the local zone, so any test asserting a literal expected string would pass or fail on the RUNNER TIMEZONE rather than on the code -- a test that measures the machine.
contributing_factors.action: The arm asserts a CLOCK COMPONENT rather than a literal, and deliberately does not assert the day, because a far-western zone moves it.

records.recurrence_open: Only the alf_claim_routes trail was checked and fixed. The same date-only-slice-of-a-server-timestamp shape may exist on other SAIRNcare panels and in other apps; nothing scans for it, and no arm would catch the next one. The credentials renderer at sairncare.html deliberately keeps a date-only render because its field is a completed_on DATE rather than a trail stamp -- that judgement was made by reading, not by a rule, so it is not protected either.

records.subject: fix(auth): a soleRole naming no real role turned the last-admin guard OFF, and the one comment describing that said the opposite
records.summary: api/_lib/employee-lifecycle.js setActive() narrows the last-admin count to [soleRole] when an app names one, and nothing validated that the name was a real provisioning role. THE FAILURE WAS PERMISSIVE, which is the opposite of what the only comment describing the scenario said: guardRoles matches no row, activeProvisioners counts ZERO, and the refusal condition ALSO tests guardRoles.indexOf(target.role) !== -1 -- false for every real row -- so the branch is UNREACHABLE. Driven against the real engine before the fix: roster of one post.govern and one post.govern.deputy, soleRole 'post.governor' (one letter), caller the deputy, target the governor, result 200 WITH THE PATCH SENT. The licence reaches zero governors and bootstrap still 409s because it does not filter on active, which is the SD-AUDIT-2026 loss reached through a typo rather than through a missing guard. Five endpoints pass this value as a hand-written literal that must agree with a role vocabulary kept in ROLES_BY_APP, in each schema check constraint and in each app's capability list. Now refused 500 GUARD_MISCONFIGURED before the roster is read, as a RETURN rather than a throw because every endpoint's catch would relabel a throw 502 'Upstream connection error -- try again'.

injection.subject: feat(sairnfreedom): per-employee credentials end to end -- and setup could empty a post of its last governor, on every app

records.citation_note: ARGUABLE and close. 1.11 is a check that cannot run being folded into a pass. Here the check RAN, on a set that could not contain its subject, and produced a pass -- could-not-answer folded into permitted, one level in from tool availability. The fix is the rule's prescription exactly: say which value is wrong, say the check did not run, and fail.

contributing_factors.factor: The guard narrows to a set built from one caller-supplied string, and both the count and the membership test are derived from that same set -- so a wrong value makes the guard vacuous rather than wrong, and a vacuous guard is indistinguishable from a satisfied one at every call site.
contributing_factors.action: soleRole is validated against provisioningRoles before anything else happens, and a mismatch is refused 500 GUARD_MISCONFIGURED naming the bad value and the real roles

contributing_factors.factor: The value is a hand-written literal repeated in five endpoints and has to agree with a role vocabulary kept in three other places. Nothing generates any of them from any other.
contributing_factors.action: generate the schema check constraint and each app capability list from ROLES_BY_APP rather than maintaining four copies; recorded, not done here

contributing_factors.factor: The only place on the platform that named this scenario described the OPPOSITE consequence -- a static arm told its reader the guard would refuse every deactivation, the over-restrictive failure. A reader who hit it and believed it would have treated a trapdoor as an inconvenience.
contributing_factors.action: the arm message and mutation 3 of the existing sabotage probe are both corrected to the permissive direction, and six new arms drive it rather than asserting it in prose

contributing_factors.factor: The existing static arm parses const SOLE_ROLE and the call site with a regex and covers only endpoints with MORE THAN ONE provisioning role, so a single-role endpoint, a non-literal value or a spelling the regex misses were all invisible.
contributing_factors.action: the validation is at runtime in the shared engine, which is where the behaviour is actually decided, and covers all ten callers rather than the parseable subset

records.recurrence_open: Only soleRole is validated. provisioningRoles, roleLabel and table are also caller-supplied strings the engine trusts, and a wrong provisioningRoles would refuse every caller (loud) while a wrong table would read an empty roster and make every guard vacuous in the same silent direction as this defect. Neither was audited here.

records.subject: fix(hover): a sha the auditor CITED was counted as one it CLAIMS -- attribution gains a third state
records.summary: tools/hover_separation_audit.py OWN_COMMIT_RE matched a sha inside hover1's quotation of cody's status line (entry 404), so a commit the auditor CITED was reported as a SEPARATION VIOLATION against cc's 270c60ed. Fixed by giving the verdict a third state (OWN/CITED/DISPUTED) requiring two independent signals to suppress, rather than narrowing the regex -- a narrowed rule fails silently on the next phrasing, and in an attribution audit a false negative is invisible.

injection.subject: feat(process): the hover auditor's separation becomes mechanical -- and both alleged breaches did not happen

records.citation_note: 1.2 is about grep not telling code from text that DESCRIBES code. This is the same shape one step over: OWN_COMMIT_RE could not tell the log's own statement from the log QUOTING another session's statement. Arguable rather than clean because 1.2's worked example is source-vs-comment, not speaker attribution inside prose.
records.phase_note: Design, not coding: the regex does exactly what it was written to do. What was wrong was the decision to treat one phrase match as an attribution verdict, which was made when the tool was designed and is stated in its own comment.

contributing_factors.factor: OWN_COMMIT_RE keyed on the phrase committed/pushed <sha> alone. That answers 'does this text say it' and was read as 'does this log claim it', which are different questions the regex has no way to tell apart.
contributing_factors.action: Attribution now has three states (OWN/CITED/DISPUTED). The regex is unchanged on purpose; the VERDICT gained the distinction the regex cannot make.

contributing_factors.factor: The self-log's summary field carries both the auditor's own statements and verbatim quotations of other sessions' status lines, with no structural marker separating them. Every reader of that field has to infer the speaker.
contributing_factors.note: Not fixed here, and not fixable from this clone: adding a speaker field to the self-log would change the hover clone's own record format, which a build agent must not touch. Flagged to hover1 and hover2 instead.

contributing_factors.factor: Nothing exercised the attribution step for over a year of entries: while the multi-log defect made both tools refuse, the code path was never reached, so the false positive existed without being reportable.
contributing_factors.action: tests/run_hover_separation_probe.py section G, 14 arms, drives _selflog_one directly with synthetic chained logs -- including the same real out-of-scope sha claimed unambiguously (violation still reported) and quoted-plus-audited (not a violation), so the fix cannot be confused with disarming the tool.

records.recurrence_open: The two suppression signals are not shown to be independent -- they agreed exactly once in 415 entries and disagreed never, which is one data point, not a measurement. And there is exactly ONE real citation-shaped match on this platform, so the criteria are locked against synthetic fixtures rather than validated against a population. A citation phrased without a quotation and without a ref entry is still classified OWN and would still produce a false violation.

records.subject: fix(sairnlaw): the trust panel said "all three balances match" from one leg that CANNOT fail and one that was never made
records.summary: sairnlaw.html trust panel rendered 'Reconciled -- all three balances match' on IOLTA client trust money from a verdict that could not fail. reconcileTrust() computed ledgerVsClient by comparing a ledger total against a per-client sum that PARTITIONS THE SAME ARRAY -- including the rows with no client_id, which form their own group and are summed like any other -- so leg one was a tautology disturbed only by float summation order. ledgerVsBank was null until a bank statement was entered and matches read null as agreement, so a firm that had never entered a statement saw a green THREE-WAY verdict with no third leg and no falsifiable second one. The dashboard suppressed its Trust Alert on the same value, reporting 'Nothing needs attention' precisely when nothing had been checked. api/_lib/law-trust-reconcile.js -- the correct reconciler, written to replace exactly this function and naming it by line number -- existed and was never called: the only occurrence of 'law_trust_reconcile' in the app was a code comment.

injection.unknown_reason: The tautological reconcileTrust() predates the reconciler that replaced it; git log -S on ledgerVsClient would name a commit, but the DEFECT is the pair (tautology retained + replacement unwired) and the second half has no single introducing commit -- api/_lib/law-trust-reconcile.js was added correct and simply never called.

records.citation_note: PR 1.11 is the nearest standing rule (a check reporting a pass it never performed) but it is about a check failing OPEN when a dependency is absent. This is a verdict that is arithmetically incapable of the value it claims to test for, plus a correct replacement that shipped unwired. The fabricated-KPI rule is about numbers with no function behind them; this is a BOOLEAN with a function behind it that can only return true.

contributing_factors.factor: A unit test on the engine cannot see an absent caller. tests/law_trust_reconcile_probe.py was GREEN the whole time the panel was broken
contributing_factors.action: tests/law_trust_reconcile_wiring_probe.py added -- 13 arms, 4 of which mutate a copy to put the defect back and assert the probe refuses it

contributing_factors.factor: The verdict was computed from two quantities derived from one array, so no test data could ever make it false
contributing_factors.action: The verdict is now the server engine status; the client function is renamed trustFigures() and returns figures only -- the rename makes a missed caller throw instead of reading a stale matches

contributing_factors.factor: null was read as agreement. An uncompared leg and an agreeing leg were the same value
contributing_factors.action: The server engine refuses a single boolean and returns AGREES/DISAGREES/PARTIAL/CANNOT_RECONCILE; the UI adds UNAVAILABLE and none of the four non-AGREES states renders as agreement

contributing_factors.factor: A correct replacement was built and the wiring was left for later, with nothing recording that it was outstanding
contributing_factors.action: Not closed here. The general question -- what records that a built engine has no caller -- is wider than this resource. cc had already found this specific instance and logged it as a review obligation rather than a defect; that routing is what left it open.

records.recurrence_open: The wiring probe covers THIS engine. Nothing enumerates the other api/_lib/ engines to ask which of them have no caller, and that is the class rather than the instance.

records.subject: fix(claims): an identifier is matched WHOLE or not at all -- an ISO timestamp was becoming the words 2026, 22t12 and 38z
records.summary: tools/sairn_claim.py tokenised structured identifiers as prose, so two Tier A discharge claims opened ONE MINUTE apart were refused on `shared phrase "2026 22t12"`, a bigram of the ISO-8601 obligation id, while their work ran in opposite directions over disjoint file sets. Commit shas were not compared at all in either direction. Fixed by stripping identifiers before tokenising and comparing timestamps and shas WHOLE as their own signal; a bare date is dropped rather than promoted, because promoting it would collide every same-day claim.

injection.subject: fix(claims): a brief restatement of an active claim no longer answers CLEAR

records.citation_note: 1.2 is grep not telling code from text describing code. This is the same inability one step over: the matcher could not tell a structured identifier from ordinary prose. Arguable rather than clean, because 1.2's worked example is source-vs-comment.
records.phase_note: Design rather than coding: the split is doing exactly what it was written to do, and the fault is that the matcher had no concept of an identifier distinct from a word. Inferred rather than stated -- the tokeniser predates the claim format that carries obligation ids, so the omission was never a decision anybody recorded.

contributing_factors.factor: word_seq() split on [^a-z0-9]+, so a structured identifier was shredded into word fragments. An ISO-8601 timestamp became the words 2026, 22t12 and 38z, and a bigram straddling two of them read as a shared phrase between two unrelated claims.
contributing_factors.action: Timestamps, shas and bare dates are stripped before tokenising; timestamps and shas are compared WHOLE as their own signal, a bare date is dropped entirely.

contributing_factors.factor: A commit sha was not compared at all, in either direction -- 'revert 467baf74' against 'extend 467baf74' answered CLEAR. The matcher had no notion of an identifier, so the strongest available evidence of two sessions working on one item was the one signal it did not use.
contributing_factors.action: shared_structured() compares shas whole, with a short sha matching its own longer form so that writing the full 40 characters is not punished.

contributing_factors.factor: The incentive was inverted on the field the tool most needs filled in honestly: an obligation id is the one token a discharge claim must carry to be identifiable, so naming the item more precisely made a refusal more likely, and the workaround it invited -- dropping or fuzzing the id -- is worse than the block.
contributing_factors.action: Named as sairn-code-scrubber item 25 with all three instances dated, and the reasoning is written into sairn_claim.py beside the rule rather than only in the register.

contributing_factors.factor: Nothing exercised an identifier at all. The matcher's control corpus is 17 hand-written pairs of prose task strings, and not one of them carried a timestamp, a sha or a date -- so the tokenisation could shred identifiers with every arm green.
contributing_factors.action: 12 arms added in both directions, plus a regression arm that re-runs the entire existing 17-case corpus through the changed tokenisation so a fix that cleared this case by breaking a real block would fail loudly.

records.recurrence_open: The identifier vocabulary is a CLOSED LIST of three shapes -- ISO timestamp, hex sha, bare date. A fourth kind of id (an issue number, a PR reference, an app-prefixed resource key written without its usual punctuation) is still shredded into words, and nothing announces that: the failure looks exactly like an ordinary word collision. And the sha rule requires a digit to avoid eating `defaced`, so a genuine all-hex digitless sha -- about four in ten thousand -- is still treated as prose.

records.subject: fix(hover): a log quoting ITSELF satisfied both suppression signals -- the quote signal now requires speaker ATTRIBUTION
records.summary: tools/hover_separation_audit.py classify_own_commit(): both suppression signals were containment tests that never asked WHO was being quoted, so a log quoting ITSELF satisfied both and an out-of-scope commit the log claimed in its own words was suppressed to zero violations. Found jointly by hover1 and hover2 and reproduced two ways before being acted on. The quote signal now requires the sentence to attribute the quotation to a different session; identity is taken from the owning directory.

injection.subject: fix(status): --note APPENDS by default; --note-replace is the explicit override -- the field that ate two real messages

records.citation_note: Same citation as the defect this was fixing, one level up: the classifier could not tell the log's own words from the log quoting somebody. Arguable rather than clean -- 1.2's worked example is code-vs-comment and this is speaker identity inside prose.
records.phase_note: Design. The classifier does exactly what its stated rule says; the rule never mentioned the speaker. The defect entered with the three-state design itself, which is why the injection commit is the fix that introduced classify_own_commit().

contributing_factors.factor: The quote signal tested CONTAINMENT -- is the match inside a balanced quotation -- and read that as evidence of another speaker. Position was standing in for identity, and the reason string said so in terms: 'so it is another session speaking and not this log', asserted having never checked.
contributing_factors.action: The quote signal now requires ATTRIBUTION: the nearest speaker marker in the sentence before the opening quote must name a session other than the log being read. Identity comes from the owning directory, never from the entry.

contributing_factors.factor: Both suppression signals were containment tests over the same entry, so requiring TWO to agree bought much less independence than it appeared to. A single self-quotation satisfies both at once.
contributing_factors.action: The third check is an identity test rather than a fourth containment test, so the signals are no longer degenerate. Stated in the code beside the rule.

contributing_factors.factor: The author's own fixtures were written from the rule as stated, and the rule as stated never mentioned the speaker -- so no fixture could have caught it. The gap was recorded in the first fix's own recurrence_open as 'the two signals are not shown to be independent' and left as an open uncertainty rather than driven.
contributing_factors.action: Seven arms G15-G21 drive attribution in both directions, including G18 as the control and G19/G20 where the same sentence classifies differently depending on which log is being read. Found by hover1 and hover2 jointly, not by the author.

records.recurrence_open: The lead-in is bounded by the sentence, so a self-marker one sentence back reports 'attributes it to nobody' rather than 'to this log itself' -- same safe verdict, less precise wording, pinned by arm G16b. And the attribution vocabulary is a CLOSED LIST of session names: a new session, or a quotation that attributes by role rather than by name ('the build agent reported'), attributes to nobody and falls to DISPUTED. That is the safe direction, but it means the rule degrades quietly as the platform's cast changes and nothing announces it.

records.subject: fix(controls): two literal BACKSPACE bytes where \b was meant -- arm 5b was passing vacuously
records.summary: tests/confidentiality_flagger_asymmetry_review_probe.py carried two raw 0x08 BACKSPACE bytes where regex word boundaries were meant, so the keyword-count pattern could never match, the count was always zero, and arm 5b passed vacuously on any input -- including the lexer desync it was written to detect. Caught by the control-character push gate, not by the author.

injection.subject: fix(flagger): client_restricted() asks what the gate is ATTACHED to, not what is nearby -- and two fail-open bugs the fix itself introduced

records.citation_note: 1.1 is a check that stopped checking, which is exactly this: the arm ran, exited green, and tested nothing. Clean citation.
records.phase_note: Design. Each piece did what its stated rule said; the rule was the wrong question -- proximity standing in for attachment.

contributing_factors.factor: The line was built through a shell heredoc and one level of backslash escaping was consumed, leaving a raw 0x08 byte where a regex word boundary was meant.
contributing_factors.action: Rebuilt with chr(92), which is what the gate's own message prescribes.

contributing_factors.factor: The arm still PASSED with the broken pattern: the keyword count was always 0, so the ratio was len(spans)/1 and the comparison succeeded on any input -- including the lexer desync the arm exists to detect.
contributing_factors.action: Confirmed by comparing against a separate measurement script that had a correct word boundary throughout: 0.59 minimum ratio both ways after the fix.

records.recurrence_open: Nothing stops the same heredoc from eating the next backslash; the push gate is the only thing that catches it, and it catches the BYTE rather than the vacuous pass. An arm whose pattern silently stops matching still reports green, and no check measures whether an arm's regex matched anything at all.

records.subject: fix(criticality): a row with an INVENTED tier matched neither branch and was dropped in silence
records.summary: criticality_tier_check.py parse(): the rollup-vs-resource disambiguator was spelled ^\*\*([ABC])\*\*$, so a resource row carrying an INVENTED tier (| `sd_invoices` | **CRITICAL** |) matched neither branch -- not a resource row because the letter is wrong, not a rollup row because cell 1 is not a bare integer -- and was dropped in silence. The BAD TIER check, which exists to stop a second tier vocabulary starting, became unreachable by exactly the rows it was written for, and the register reported the resource as having NO ROW rather than a wrong one.

injection.subject: feat(criticality): step 1 of the two-axis migration -- the parser, both shapes, and the mis-parse found before a row moved

records.citation_note: No standing rule names 'a disambiguator narrowed to the valid vocabulary makes the invalid-vocabulary check unreachable'. Closest is PR 1.11 (a check that reports a pass it never performed), but that one is about a MISSING dependency, not about a parser silently discarding its own subject.

contributing_factors.factor: The disambiguator and the validator were written to the same vocabulary, so narrowing one silently narrowed what the other could ever see
contributing_factors.action: RESOURCE_CELL1 now matches any bold token; validating the letter stays with BAD TIER, which is the only place it belongs

contributing_factors.factor: parse() drops an unrecognised row rather than reporting it, so a mis-parse is indistinguishable from an absent row
contributing_factors.action: Report a row whose cell 0 is a backticked name and which matches neither branch as UNREADABLE ROW instead of skipping it. Not done here -- scoped out deliberately so this fix stays the one-line disambiguator change the probe proved.

contributing_factors.factor: The change landed in the same session that wrote it, with the probe not re-run before commit -- arm 4 would have caught it immediately
contributing_factors.action: Both criticality probes now run before commit on this file, and arm 4 is green

records.recurrence_open: The actions close THIS narrowing. They do not close the general shape: any other consumer of the register that anchors on the valid vocabulary rather than on row structure can lose a row the same way, and nothing enumerates those consumers.

records.subject: fix(sairnvet): 41 tables including the DEA-relevant controlled-substance register were readable and writable on a bare licence key
records.summary: api/sd-data.js dispatched all 41 SV_RESOURCES entries -- including sv_controlled, the DEA-relevant controlled-substance register, plus sv_patients and sv_soapnotes -- with NO session check on either verb. The licence key is a BEARER CREDENTIAL shipped to the browser and readable by anyone who can open the app, so it was the entire boundary on the clinical record. REPRODUCED LIVE WITH A CONTROL before the fix was applied, because an unmigrated table answers an honest empty to everybody and that is not a gate: sairncare/alf_mar and sairncare/alf_claim_routes answered 401 NO_SESSION on a bare key, while sairnvet/sv_controlled, sv_patients, sv_soapnotes and sv_whiteboard all answered 200 with provisioned:true on identical treatment. STATED RATHER THAN GLOSSED: every open table returned ZERO ROWS on the tenant I drove (SV-PINNACLE-2026), so my run demonstrated that nothing stops a caller REACHING the resource rather than that regulated data left; hover2's reproduction on their tenant did return rows. THE INJECTION COMMIT IS 29b1f1d5 AND THAT NEEDS SAYING: the dispatcher's own comment -- 'SAIRNvet has no per-employee authentication at all ... a session gate here would gate on a session that does not exist' -- was TRUE when written. 29b1f1d5 shipped api/sv-auth.js, ROLES_BY_APP.sairnvet, AUTH_TABLE_BY_APP.sairnvet and the schema on 2026-09-13, under the subject line 'the last app without it held the DEA register', and nothing re-read the justification after the premise it rested on stopped holding. The absence became a defect at that moment, not when the dispatcher was written.

injection.subject: feat(sairnvet): per-employee auth -- the last app without it held the DEA register

records.citation_note: 2.3 is 'a fact with a tense needs a read' and it lives in Part 2, EDITING STANDING DOCUMENTS. This was a CODE COMMENT, not a standing document -- a present-tense assertion about the platform ('SAIRNvet has no per-employee authentication at all') sitting in api/sd-data.js and load-bearing, because it is the stated reason a gate is absent. Cited as the nearest true match while naming the extension rather than pretending the fit is exact: the rule as written would not have caught this, and whether it should be widened to cover justification comments is a real question this record is evidence for. Not recorded as not-citable, because the failure mode is 2.3's failure mode exactly.

contributing_factors.factor: 29b1f1d5 built the whole per-employee auth subsystem for SAIRNvet -- endpoint, role list, auth table mapping, schema -- and did not wire it into the one dispatcher that serves the app data. The subsystem existed and nothing consumed it for nine days.
contributing_factors.action: One session check before the SV_RESOURCES dispatch, so neither branch is reachable without it, scoped to sairnvet via verifySessionToken third argument, and placed BEFORE the pre-existing sv_controlled witness lock so an unauthenticated write is refused for having no session rather than merely for lacking a witness.

contributing_factors.factor: The reason the gate was absent was recorded as a present-tense code comment. A comment cannot notice that its premise expired, and this one kept reading as current documentation for nine days after it stopped being true -- to at least one other session, which cited it to reach the WRONG conclusion (cody cc7165b4) before hover2 checked the premise instead of the comment.

records.subject: fix(sairncare): derive_charges could list one day's doses differently on two identical runs -- and my own review overstated why
records.summary: api/sd-data.js derive_charges: two of its three event-source reads (alf_mar, alf_activities) carried no order= clause, and api/_lib/care-charges.js sorted the derived lines on DATE ALONE. Array.prototype.sort is stable, so same-day rows kept insertion order -- the concatenation order of the three sources, and within each source whatever order the server returned. Two identical regenerations of one month could therefore list the same day's doses in different sequences, on a table whose first column is Date. The unpriced list, rendered with dates under 'Documented but NOT billed', was not sorted at all. NO MONEY WAS WRONG: the total is a sum and reconcileAgainstInvoice keys on event_id, so both the invoice total and the regenerate-diff were order-independent throughout.

records.subject: fix(auth): the last admin could be DEMOTED instead of deactivated, on four apps hardened against deactivation hours earlier
records.summary: The last-admin guard watches DEACTIVATION and not the role change that reaches the identical end state. Every setup on this platform upserts on (license_hash, employee_id) writing the role column, so demoting the last holder of a sole role empties the licence of provisioners through a door nothing was standing at -- zero active owners, with bootstrap still answering 409 ALREADY_PROVISIONED because it deliberately does not filter on active, so there is no route back through the app. MEASURED across every api/*-auth.js: 17 setup paths, ONE carried a guard (api/sf-auth.js, written the same day by the session whose review surfaced this), 16 did not, and FOUR were REACHABLE -- api/grd-auth.js, api/sb-auth.js, api/scp-auth.js and api/sd-auth.js each declare SOLE_ROLE 'owner' (so their set_active guard counts owners only) AND each setup upserts writing role. Those four are the same apps commit 591531ce hardened against DEACTIVATION hours earlier. Closed with one shared soleRoleDemotionRefusal() in api/_lib/employee-lifecycle.js wired into all four, refusing 409 LAST_ADMIN before the write, allowing promotions and PIN resets, and refusing 500 rather than counting zero when soleRole names no real role.

records.subject: fix(deadlines): an absent period count became a legal deadline on the trigger date itself -- and the obvious guard refused a real Maryland rule
records.summary: api/_lib/deadline-engine.js read Number(x.count.value) at four sites with no check. That coercion maps a real zero, an empty string, null and an empty array all to 0, and zero is a LEGITIMATE count here (Md. Rule 2-311(b) has a zero-count limb), so an absent or malformed period count produced ok:true and a legal deadline ON THE TRIGGER DATE with a detail line reading 'counted 0 calendar days'. A non-numeric count gave NaN, addDays returned an Invalid Date, and that propagated as a date-shaped value nothing downstream questioned. NOT OBSERVED IN LIVE RULE DATA -- the reachability is through a malformed or incomplete rule definition, and no such rule is in the repo today.

injection.unknown_reason: The Number() coercion predates the multi-limb resolver and no commit introduced the gap: the guard was never present at any point in the file's history, so there is no injection commit to cite.

records.citation_note: Adjacent rather than identical: no check ran and reported a pass -- instead a coercion silently produced a value indistinguishable from a valid one, so every downstream check passed honestly on a number that meant nothing. Same family: a could-not-tell folded into an answer.

records.subject: fix(claims): the matcher decides on the DECLARED FILE SET, and the word overlap becomes a warning
records.summary: tools/sairn_claim.py decided whether two sessions collide by LEXICAL OVERLAP -- shared app word, shared identifier, shared adjacent word pair -- which is a proxy for the real question, 'would these two sessions edit the same file'. Claims began declaring FILES: <paths> on 2026-09-21, making the real question answerable, and the proxy was measured against it: over all 318 cross-session pairs among claims that declare files, the matcher BLOCKS 153 and only 43 of those have intersecting file sets. 110 blocks -- 72% -- are false, on boilerplate such as 'html tests', 'api files', 'api lib' and '2026 obligation'. One stale claim produced three of tonight's collisions against two different sessions, each costing a real stop-and-flag cycle, and one session resorted to choosing a subject slug specifically to dodge a bigram, which is the rewording PR 4.3 forbids arriving as an adaptation. Fixed: the declared file set is now the primary check (intersect -> refuse naming the path, disjoint -> no block with the lexical match printed as a warning), and a claim declaring no files falls back to the lexical matcher unchanged.

contributing_factors.action: The dependency sweep removes the class of cause; the baseline arm already reported the symptom loudly and now stops the run as well.

contributing_factors.factor: Every mutation arm asserted only 'the probe exited non-zero'. A probe that fails UNCONDITIONALLY satisfies that whatever the mutation is, so the five sabotages were reported as caught by a control that would have said the same with no mutation applied. 25 of 26 passes were vacuous, in the file whose whole subject is that a control must be shown to fail.

records.recurrence_open: The dependency sweep follows `import X` and `from X import` at the start of a line. A tool that imported a sibling dynamically -- importlib, a deferred import inside a function body indented past the regex, a name built at runtime -- would still be missed, and the failure would look exactly like this one did. And nothing on this platform scans for the SHAPE of the defect: a suite whose arms all assert the same single condition on a shared upstream artefact is vacuous the moment that artefact breaks, and only reading it finds that.

records.subject: fix(stonedesk): eleven money and count folds where `|| 0` never coerced -- one string field and the whole KPI concatenates
records.summary: stonedesk.html carried eleven uncoerced numeric folds of the shape `s + (x.field || 0)`, seven of them money: invoice totals, revenue MTD, average job margin, contractor YTD spend, waste cost and two profit calculations. `|| 0` does not coerce -- a non-empty string is truthy, so the guard never fires and `+` concatenates, turning a sum into a string from the first non-numeric row onward. Found by tools/truthy_sum_check.py via its own probe going red on the real-tree arm. REPAIRED IN PLACE 2026-09-22: three backtick spans in this summary were executed as SHELL COMMAND SUBSTITUTIONS by --add and arrived as empty strings, so the sentence read \"folds of the shape , seven of them\" and \"the guard never fires and  concatenates\". The words are restored here and the loss is recorded rather than tidied away -- tool-bugs item 5, fourth instance, and the first in defect_register.py, which has no --body-file route.

injection.unknown_reason: Eleven occurrences across four panels with no common commit; tools/truthy_sum_baseline.json grandfathered fifty-one keys on 2026-09-11 without dating any of them, and git -S on a fragment as common as `||0)` cannot separate the commit that introduced a fold from the commits that reformatted the line around it. (The backtick span here was also eaten by the shell at --add time and is restored; see the summary.)

records.citation_note: No numbered process rule covers a JavaScript coercion hazard. The nearest standing statement on this platform is the auto-memory note that a quiet wrong number beats a loud crash -- a concatenated KPI is plausible-looking and silent, which is the shape that rule is about -- but that is a memory, not a numbered section, and stretching one of the numbered rules to cover it would blur the class it actually names.

contributing_factors.factor: `|| 0` was used as if it coerced. It does not: a non-empty string is truthy, so the guard never fires and `+` concatenates. Seven of the eleven are money folds -- invoice totals, revenue month-to-date, average job margin, contractor YTD spend and two profit calculations -- where the result is a figure a shop owner reads and acts on.
contributing_factors.action: all eleven wrapped as `Number(x) || 0`, which is the idiom already present in these files. Number(x) || 0 rather than Number(x || 0) deliberately: the latter yields NaN on a non-numeric string and one bad row would take a whole KPI tile to NaN.

contributing_factors.factor: WHETHER ANY OF THE ELEVEN IS EXPLOITABLE TODAY IS NOT ESTABLISHED, and the checker's own docstring says the question -- who can write this field -- is not derivable from the fold. A field written only by app code that already coerces cannot hold a string; one written through an API branch with no domain check can, which is what dnt_vendor_orders was.
contributing_factors.action: coerced all eleven rather than asserting eleven provenance claims that cannot be checked from here. The tool's alternative remedy -- baselining a field as provably numeric -- requires exactly the claim that would have been a guess.

contributing_factors.factor: The checker and its probe both existed and both worked. What was missing is that nothing RUNS them on a cadence: truthy_sum_check.py is not a push gate and its probe is not in the promoted registry, so the eleven sat unbaselined and unreported until a sweep of fixture-building probes ran it for an unrelated reason.
contributing_factors.note: Promoting it would make every push pay for a whole-tree regex scan of eight files to guard a hazard class that is explicitly NOT ASSESSED per field. The baseline mechanism is the design: it fails on a NEW occurrence, which is what it did here as soon as somebody ran it.

records.recurrence_open: FIFTY grandfathered keys remain across eight files, every one of them carrying the words NOT ASSESSED, and this commit reduced that population by coercing eleven NEW occurrences rather than by assessing any of the fifty. The two lines immediately above the one stale entry removed here -- sairnbuild.html:5508 and 5509 -- are uncoerced money folds sitting beside a coerced one in the same function, and the checker does not fail on them because they are grandfathered.

records.citation_note: The eighth cross-domain discipline (nothing announces the day a check stops testing anything) is the closest, and this is its sub-case where the check DOES announce it -- the harness's ANCHOR-0 is exactly the loud failure that discipline asks for. The defect is that the announcement was left standing rather than acted on.

contributing_factors.factor: The mutation anchored on two adjacent STATEMENTS rather than on the condition that expresses the property
contributing_factors.action: Re-anchored on the boundary itself -- neutering the condition removes the as-of comparison and leaves the clearance tracking untouched

records.subject: fix(sairnmechanical): scanned-document text was stored and SYNCED verbatim, names and all, and the toast said it stayed on the device
records.summary: mech_docs stored and SERVER-SYNCED raw AI-extracted document text verbatim, with no redaction of any kind. sairnmechanical.html's scanDoc() asks the model, in its own words, to 'EXTRACT: Every field -- names, dates, amounts, codes, reference numbers' from photographed work orders, maintenance contracts, permits, inspection reports and INVOICES; saveDoc() then stored el.textContent unchanged as {id,date,text} and mechPushRecord pushed it to the mech_docs table. The nearest are the fabrication rules, which are about numbers with no function behind them, and this is the opposite shape -- a real function whose output was never filtered. records.subject: fix(sairncare): six append-only trail reads had no order= clause -- not three, and unordered is not insertion order
records.summary: api/sd-data.js read SIX SAIRNcare append-only trails with no order= clause -- alf_mar, alf_incidents, alf_signals, alf_claim_routes, alf_staff_credentials, alf_op_audits. Postgres promises nothing about the order of a SELECT that does not ask for one and PostgREST forwards that through, so rows came back in plan order. On a small table a seq scan usually returns heap order, which is why it looked like insertion order for the whole of development and would stop the first time the planner picked an index. WORST INSTANCE, and the one the severity is set by: prRenderRecorded maps alf_claim_routes rows straight into a table with NO client sort of any kind and renders created_at sliced to 10 characters, so the server order WAS the display order and there was none -- a billing determination trail in arbitrary order. alf_mar and alf_incidents do sort, but on a date-only jsonb field, so every same-day entry ties and falls back to server order under a stable sort. alf_staff_credentials and alf_op_audits already sorted by created_at desc client-side and were deterministic except on an exact tie. alf_signals has no consumer yet. THE INJECTION COMMIT NAMED IS f29e5f95, the claim_routes instance; the other five entered in separate commits and the lag here is that one instance's, not the class's.

injection.subject: feat: SAIRNcare Phase 1 -- payer/billing-routing engine (HCBS waiver + hospice/MA relatedness)

records.citation_note: 1.1 is cited for the DETECTION half, not for the defect itself -- an unordered read is not a check that stopped checking. tests/sairncare/test-alf-mar.js and test-alf-signals.js both assert the read URL with an UNANCHORED prefix regex that stops at '...data', so both matched identically before and after the fix. They were green throughout and could never have gone red either way, which is 1.1's shape exactly: a suite that passes on both sides of a change is not evidence about that change.

contributing_factors.factor: Six facility-wide trail reads were written with no order= clause, on the implicit assumption that PostgREST returns insertion order. It does not; it returns plan order.
contributing_factors.action: Explicit &order= added to all six reads -- created_at.desc on five, recorded_at.desc on alf_signals. Direction chosen against the consumer: every SAIRNcare renderer that sorts this data sorts newest-first.

contributing_factors.factor: Nothing on the platform checked read ordering at all, and the two suites that DO assert these URLs use unanchored prefix regexes that match either side of the change.
contributing_factors.action: api/alf-append-only-read-order.test.js (9 arms) plus tests/run_alf_read_order_sabotage_probe.py, which plants seven defects -- including the clause surviving only as a comment, and the read hoisted out of the arm sight -- and all seven are refused.

contributing_factors.factor: The work arrived scoped to THREE of the six reads. The other three were found only by enumerating the whole append-only class rather than working the list as handed over; fixing three and shipping an arm named for the class would have published an all-clear over reads it never looked at.
contributing_factors.action: The arm PARSES its table list out of the const TABLES array in api/alf-append-only-fail-closed.test.js instead of retyping it, so the scope cannot silently be three again and a seventh trail added upstream fails the arm until it is ordered too.

contributing_factors.factor: Each of these reads answers an upstream 400 with {ok:true,data:[],provisioned:false}, so an order column that does not exist in the live database would render to the user as THE TABLE IS NOT SET UP rather than as an error. That standing shape is what makes a query-syntax change here riskier than it looks.
contributing_factors.note: The 400-as-not-provisioned mapping is deliberate and load-bearing elsewhere -- it is how the client distinguishes a never-migrated table from a genuinely empty one, which was itself a 2026-09-21 fix. Narrowing it is a separate decision, not a side effect of this one. Mitigated here instead by a live read-back of all six reads against the deployed endpoint.
