records.subject: fix(sairnlaw): the dashboard was silent on a 403, and silence meant two things
records.summary: SAIRNlaw dashboard was SILENT when the trust reconciliation returned 403, so for a non-owner an empty trust row could mean either 'the reconciliation ran and agreed' or 'this control is not yours' and nothing on the dashboard distinguished them. The Trust panel said the honest sentence; the dashboard is the surface people scan and the panel is the one opened deliberately, so a role that never opened the Trust tab never met it.

injection.subject: fix: SAIRNlaw -- all 6 remaining WARNING findings

records.citation_note: No standing rule names 'a deliberate silence indistinguishable from an all-clear'. The nearest is the silent-failure family, but nothing here failed -- the control ran and correctly refused this role. The gap is that the ABSENCE of an alarm carried two meanings.
records.phase_note: The 403 branch was written deliberately, on the reasoning that a role which cannot run a control is not told about it. That is right about the RESULT and wrong about the SILENCE, so the defect is in the design decision rather than in its implementation.

contributing_factors.factor: The dashboard and the Trust panel were written as separate surfaces and only the PANEL was ever asked what a non-owner should see. The panel got a correct, explicit sentence for the 403 case; the dashboard got a branch that skipped the row entirely.
contributing_factors.action: The 403 case now paints its own row on the dashboard. Where a control has two surfaces, the question 'what does a role that cannot run this see HERE' has to be answered on each surface, not once.

contributing_factors.factor: AN OMITTED ROW HAS NO AUTHOR AND NO REVIEWER. Every other trust outcome produced a visible sentence somebody wrote and somebody could disagree with. This one produced nothing, so there was no text in the diff or on the screen for a reviewer to read.
contributing_factors.action: Both branches of the failure path now emit a row, so the not-your-control case is a sentence in the source that a reviewer can argue with rather than an early return.

contributing_factors.factor: Silence is the one UI state that cannot be inspected for correctness by looking at it. A wrong badge is visible; a missing row is indistinguishable from a healthy one, and on THIS panel a missing row means 'nothing needs attention'.
contributing_factors.action: Recorded as the generalisable shape rather than fixed here: on any dashboard whose empty state reads as an all-clear, a deliberate non-render needs the same scrutiny as a rendered claim. Not turned into a checker -- no mechanical test can tell an intended omission from an unintended one.
contributing_factors.note: Not actionable as a CHECK, and that is the decision rather than a deferral. A deliberate non-render and an accidental one are byte-identical, so no static tool can separate them, and a tool that flagged every early return on a dashboard would produce noise nobody reads. It is recorded as a SHAPE to carry into review instead: on a surface whose empty state reads as an all-clear, an omission is a claim and needs the same scrutiny as a rendered one.

records.recurrence_open: Every other SAIRN dashboard that hides a row a role cannot act on is unexamined. This fix is one surface in one app -- nothing was swept, and no checker can find the shape, because a deliberate non-render and an accidental one are byte-identical. The recurrence question is open across the platform and is stated here rather than implied closed by a single corrective action.

records.subject: fix(sairnvet): the no-fallback check's comment stripper is a scanner, not a regex -- a `//` inside a string took the rest of the line
records.summary: The comment stripper in api/sairnvet-transcribe.test.js could hide the code the check exists to find. The no-fallback check strips comments before asserting that the SAIRNvet scribe module contains no reference to the browser SpeechRecognition API -- the module's own header names that API in order to reject it, so stripping is necessary. The stripper was two regexes, and the line-comment one guarded `//` with `[^:]`, which protects `http://` and nothing else: a `//` inside a STRING, REGEX or TEMPLATE literal took the entire rest of that line with it, including any SpeechRecognition reference after it. So a real fallback branch written after a string containing `//` on the same line would have passed the ban. Replaced with a character scanner tracking string/template/regex/line-comment/block-comment state, because whether a `/` opens a comment, opens a regex or is a division depends on what came before it and that is a state machine rather than a pattern. MEASURED LATENT AT THE TIME: no line in the shipped scribe module had the dangerous shape, so nothing was actually hidden -- that is a property of the source, not of the check, and the next module is not obliged to keep it.

injection.subject: feat(sairnvet): the ambient scribe -- consent flow, capture UI and a transcription contract that refuses every request, which is the feature

records.citation_note: 1.2 is "Grep cannot tell code from text that describes code" and this is the same boundary failing in the other direction: the tool that exists to tell them apart could not, so it removed CODE while trying to remove TEXT. Cited as arguable rather than clean because 1.2's incidents are about a check reading prose AS code, and this one read code AS prose -- same distinction, opposite error, and no section states the converse directly.

contributing_factors.factor: A lexical question -- is this `/` a comment, a regex or a division -- was answered with a regex, which cannot carry the state the answer depends on
contributing_factors.action: replaced with a character scanner tracking string, template, regex, line-comment and block-comment state; the one remaining heuristic (regex vs division by previous meaningful character) is named in the source and fails LOUD rather than silent

contributing_factors.factor: The shipped fixture tested four cases and every one of them was a shape the regex handled; nothing in it attacked the guard clause itself
contributing_factors.action: the fixture now carries nine cases -- five attacks including the two that defeated V1, four comment shapes -- plus a paired positive arm that fails a stripper which passes the attacks by doing nothing

contributing_factors.factor: The defect was invisible to every check that mattered because the source it was pointed at happened not to contain the dangerous shape, so a green suite was evidence about the module rather than about the checker
contributing_factors.note: No action: a rule that every source-reading check must be driven against adversarial fixtures rather than only against the live source would be real, but writing one off a single instance is over-fitting. Recorded as a factor so a second instance has something to join.

records.recurrence_open: The scanner is not a parser. Regex-versus-division is still decided by the previous meaningful character, which is the standard heuristic and can be wrong on exotic input; the failure direction is a FALSE REPORT rather than a hidden reference, and a fixture drives that direction, but it is not a proof. Nothing prevents the same regex-for-a-lexical-question shape appearing in another source-reading check on this platform, and several exist.

records.subject: fix(stonedesk): the visualizer's slab picker listed a session-cached array -- a slab another device reserved still showed in-stock and a metered render was spent on it
records.summary: StoneDesk's photo-to-quote visualizer listed slabs from sdSlabs, the localStorage array, filtered to status:'in-stock'. The filter is right; the input is not. slabSyncFromSupabase() runs only from loadSlabs(), behind the _slabLoaded once-per-session guard, so the picker showed whatever was cached when the app started. A slab another device reserved an hour earlier still read in-stock. THE DOUBLE SALE WAS NEVER THE EXPOSURE and that is why this looked closed: api/sd-data.js's slabs/reserve branch is a real compare-and-swap that refuses a conflict with 409 and uses a plain INSERT rather than the write branch's upsert, so two devices racing an unsynced slab collide on the unique index. What a stale list costs is a METERED render -- the panel tracks viz-kpi-used/cap/left, so a rep picks the held slab, SPENDS a render showing the customer their kitchen in that stone, and only finds out at Quote This. The money is safe; the render and the conversation are not. Fixed by awaiting the sync before listing, and by giving slabSyncFromSupabase() a {ok, reason} return so a failed or empty refresh renders the cached list WITH a line saying the reservations on it may be out of date rather than silently passing it off as current.

injection.subject: feat: Visualize on Your Kitchen -- photo upload + AI material-swap render (Phase 1)

contributing_factors.factor: vizRenderSlabList() filtered sdSlabs, the localStorage array, which slabSyncFromSupabase() only ever refreshes from loadSlabs() behind the _slabLoaded once-per-session guard. The filter was correct; its input was as old as app start.
contributing_factors.action: the picker now awaits slabSyncFromSupabase() before it lists

contributing_factors.factor: the _slabLoaded guard is CORRECT for the slab module -- its own comment says the flag belongs to the load, not to one of its callers -- and a second consumer in a different panel inherited that once-per-session lifetime without ever deciding it wanted one.
contributing_factors.action: sweep every other reader of sdSlabs for the same inherited once-per-session lifetime, and decide per reader whether it wants one -- not yet run; this fix covers the visualizer only

contributing_factors.factor: slabSyncFromSupabase() ended in catch(e){} and returned undefined, so a caller could not distinguish a confirmed list from a cached one -- there was no third state to check even if somebody had thought to.
contributing_factors.action: it now returns {ok, reason}, and the empty-array branch is reported rather than counted as a sync

contributing_factors.factor: the server-side compare-and-swap was built first and is correct, which made the feature read as closed. The reviewed question was 'can two devices sell one slab' -- answered, no -- and not 'what does a rep see before they get there'.
contributing_factors.note: no check catches a correct guard placed one step later than the cost it was meant to prevent; the register entry is the record

records.recurrence_open: This fixes the ONE reader. Nothing enforces that a future panel reading sdSlabs refreshes first, and nothing measures how often a rep actually hits a stale row -- so the frequency this was worth fixing at is still unmeasured.

records.subject: fix(sairnvet): the scribe preflight decides availability POSITIVELY -- a lapsed licence no longer enables the button that asks a client to consent
records.summary: scribePreflight() in sairnvet.html decided ambient-scribe availability by the ABSENCE of one failure code -- "anything that is NOT TRANSCRIBE_HOST_NOT_CONFIGURED means a host IS configured" -- which is an allowlist written as a denylist. Driven against the real endpoint: with a host configured, a VALID licence answers the preflight body with 400 CONSENT_REF_REQUIRED and an INVALID one answers 403 LICENSE_INVALID, and the old rule enabled the "Start - ask the client" consent button for BOTH. So a practice whose licence had lapsed, or whose host was configured and broken, reached the point of asking a client to consent to a recording that could never be transcribed -- the harm the module's own header names as consent theatre. Corrected to decide POSITIVELY from CONSENT_REF_REQUIRED, the only code that proves host AND licence AND app together, because the endpoint checks them in that order. LATENT AT THE TIME OF THE FIX: hostConfigured() is false in every environment, so the branch could not execute -- the wrong logic was shipped, the wrong behaviour was not, and the severity reflects that rather than the harm the code describes.

injection.subject: feat(sairnvet): the ambient scribe -- consent flow, capture UI and a transcription contract that refuses every request, which is the feature

records.citation_note: Cited against 1.11 by ANALOGY and the analogy is stated rather than implied: 1.11 is about a CHECK that must fail closed when a tool it depends on is absent, and this is a CLIENT deciding a capability is available when the server told it something it did not understand. The shared rule is the one 1.11 names -- "could not tell" is a third state and is never folded into a pass -- and the preflight folded four distinct refusals into one pass. No section in the process rules covers a client-side availability decision directly, which is itself worth noticing.

contributing_factors.factor: The availability rule was written as a denylist -- one named failure meant unavailable, everything else meant available -- in a file where every other refusal is an explicit allowlist entry
contributing_factors.action: scribePreflight() now decides positively from CONSENT_REF_REQUIRED, the only code that proves host and licence and app together; every other answer is shown with the endpoint's own structured message

contributing_factors.factor: The endpoint's refusals were designed as a NAMED set and the client consumed them as an UNNAMED remainder, so the two halves of one contract were built to opposite conventions by the same session in the same change
contributing_factors.note: No action taken: a convention that structured refusals must be consumed by name would be a real rule, but writing one off a single instance is the over-fitting this platform records elsewhere. Recorded as a factor so a second instance has something to join.

contributing_factors.factor: Nothing drove the preflight against a CONFIGURED host, because hostConfigured() is false in every environment and the suite tested the shipped state rather than the state the feature is for
contributing_factors.action: tests/sairnvet_scribe_review_probe.js drives the endpoint with SAIRNVET_TRANSCRIBE_URL set, which is how both halves were found; arm A1b is now the regression guard and arm C0 re-locates the client rule in the page so the probe cannot silently drift from it

records.recurrence_open: The fix closes the LICENCE half and not the LIVENESS half: the preflight is answered locally, so a host that is configured and UNREACHABLE still reads as available and the consent button still enables. Proving liveness means calling a transcription host on every panel render, which is a design decision with a real cost rather than a one-line correction, and it is measured and stated in arm A1d rather than implied away. Nothing yet prevents the same denylist shape appearing in another client that consumes a structured-refusal endpoint.

records.subject: fix(money): the profit subtraction coerced one operand and not the other -- and un-grandfathering it exposed a THIRD tax surface nobody had looked at
records.summary: StoneDesk's profit figure coerced one operand of a subtraction and not the other. de7b4838 wrapped the invoices half in Number() and left the bills half -- bills.reduce(s + (b.amt || 0)) -- untouched ON THE SAME LINE, at stonedesk.html:36531 and :36544. DRIVEN, NOT REASONED: bills of "100" and "200" fold to the STRING "0100200", so profit reports -99450 where 450 is right. A string sum inside a subtraction produces an arbitrary negative rather than merely appending, which is why this is worse than an uncoerced sum alone. BOTH CONSUMERS STATE THE NUMBER AS FACT RATHER THAN DISPLAYING IT: sdTaxCalc posts it to /api/claude as "Actual tracked data: revenue minus expenses (profit) of $X" and asks for estimated annual liability, quarterly schedule and 1099 obligations; sdTaxPrint prints it on a Tax Report where Math.max(0, profit*0.28) turns the negative into $0 rather than NaN, silently understating tax on a document a shop hands a CPA. The same function's salesTaxYTD was uncoerced too -- entries of "50" and "25" fold to "05025", which Math.round makes 5025, so $75 prints as "$5,025": not an error, a plausible wrong number two orders of magnitude out. FOUND BY INDEPENDENT REVIEW of the very commit that introduced it, while discharging that commit's Tier A obligation. Both fields were in truthy_sum_baseline.json's grandfathered map so truthy_sum_check.py exited 0 and printed CLEAN throughout; removing them immediately exposed a THIRD tax surface -- taxRender(), drawing panel-tax's KPI tiles -- with three more uncoerced folds, one of which the checker structurally cannot detect because it has no fallback at all. Six folds fixed, two baseline entries removed, and api/sd-data.js's invoices write branch now refuses a non-numeric amount with 400 INVALID_AMOUNT so the input cannot reach storage in the first place.

injection.subject: fix(stonedesk): eleven money and count folds where `|| 0` never coerced -- one string field and the whole KPI concatenates

records.citation_note: Rule 1.5 is about a confident line printed after an error, and here nothing errors at all. The kinship is exact in CONSEQUENCE rather than in mechanism: a figure that is wrong is printed as a tax estimate and asserted to an LLM as tracked data, with no failure anywhere for anyone to notice. Cited as arguable rather than clean, because the rule's own mechanism -- a return value nobody reads -- is absent.

contributing_factors.factor: de7b4838 coerced the INVOICES half of `profit = invoices.reduce(...) - bills.reduce(...)` and left the BILLS half uncoerced on the same line. A string sum inside a subtraction does not append, it produces an arbitrary negative: bills of "100" and "200" fold to "0100200" and profit reports -99450 where 450 is right.
contributing_factors.action: all six money folds across the three tax surfaces coerced with Number(x)||0

contributing_factors.factor: stonedesk.html::b.amt and ::e.tax were both in truthy_sum_baseline.json's grandfathered map, so truthy_sum_check.py exited 0 and printed CLEAN for the whole period. The tool built to find exactly this class could not see it BY CONFIGURATION rather than by capability.
contributing_factors.action: both entries removed by name; the suite asserts the count went 48 to 46 and that no third entry left in passing

contributing_factors.factor: A THIRD tax surface carried the identical defect and nobody had looked: taxRender(), drawing panel-tax's KPI tiles, had three more uncoerced folds. Its first one -- `s + i.amount` with no `|| 0` at all -- is STRUCTURALLY INVISIBLE to the checker, whose pattern is `+ (x || 0)`. It was found by clearing a baseline entry, not by searching.
contributing_factors.action: the no-guard fold shape (`s + x` with no fallback) is not detectable by truthy_sum_check at all; widening it to that shape is a separate change and is NOT made here -- named so the gap is known rather than assumed covered

contributing_factors.factor: api/sd-data.js's invoices write branch validated payload.id and payload.customer_id and stored the rest of the payload verbatim as a jsonb blob, so a string amount could reach storage in the first place. Coercing on read repairs the readers that exist and does nothing for the next one.
contributing_factors.action: 400 INVALID_AMOUNT when amount is present and not a finite number; absent and null still accepted, measured against the one live caller

contributing_factors.factor: Both consumers state the figure as FACT rather than displaying it. sdTaxCalc posts it to /api/claude as "Actual tracked data" and asks for tax liability and 1099 obligations; sdTaxPrint prints it on a Tax Report where Math.max(0, profit*0.28) turns a negative into $0 rather than NaN. That is what turns a wrong total into an understated tax figure instead of a visibly broken tile.
contributing_factors.note: no check asks whether a computed number is about to be asserted to an LLM or printed as a tax figure; the clamp is correct in isolation and only harmful downstream of bad input, which is now fixed at both ends

records.recurrence_open: The checker still cannot see a fold with NO fallback at all. Its pattern is the truthy-guard shape, plus (x || 0); taxRender's invTotal was the bare shape, s + i.amount, and was invisible to it by construction rather than by configuration. Widening truthy_sum_check.py to that shape is a separate change and was NOT made here, so the gap is named rather than assumed covered. AND 46 GRANDFATHERED ENTRIES REMAIN: each is a hazard nobody has assessed, and this defect is the first demonstration that the list hides real ones rather than only theoretical ones -- two of its entries were a live money bug on a tax report.

records.subject: fix(sairncode): SIXTEEN Tier A resources were writable on the licence key alone and hard-deletable, for eight days
records.summary: SAIRNcode's Tier A write gate and soft-delete list both derive from one array in api/_resources/sairncode.js, and that array still held the seven names it was given on 2026-09-15 while docs/CRITICALITY-TIERS.md had grown to 23 Tier A sc_* rows. For eight days the sixteen in between accepted a write carrying the LICENCE KEY ALONE -- no employee session -- and could be hard-deleted: sc_anesthesia, sc_anesthesia_base_units, sc_auth, sc_auth_requests, sc_coded_items, sc_dme, sc_drg, sc_eligibility, sc_fraud, sc_hcc, sc_prebill, sc_providers, sc_query, sc_rac, sc_settings, sc_telehealth. Three of them are the reason this is critical rather than bookkeeping: sc_hcc is a named patient joined to a diagnosis grouping and its dollar value, sc_eligibility is a named patient joined to payer and plan, and sc_providers carries the QP status that selects between two CMS CY2026 conversion factors -- so a caller holding the licence string the app documents as NOT being auth could change what every unit billed under that provider is worth. The derivation was correct and the thing it derived from was stale, which is why every downstream gate was wrong at once.

injection.unknown_reason: No single commit injected it: the array was correct when written on 2026-09-15 and became wrong as sixteen register rows were re-tiered A by four sessions between 2026-09-15 and 2026-09-23. The defect is the absence of a link between those re-tiers and this array, not any one of them.

records.citation_note: The pin fired and nothing made anybody look. tests/sairncode_gates.js asserts this array equals the Tier A sc_* rows in docs/CRITICALITY-TIERS.md in BOTH directions, and it had been RED for eight days saying exactly which sixteen were missing. It is not in GUARD_TESTS, so its red never blocked a push, and no hook or suite invokes it. That is a different failure from an absent check: the mechanism worked and the requirement to read it did not exist.
records.phase_note: It was not introduced in a phase -- it accrued. The code shipped correct and the document it derives from moved underneath it sixteen times.
records.factors_unknown_reason: Named in the obligation body opened against a49edd00 and not yet worked through by an independent session: the pin is report-only, the suite is not in GUARD_TESTS, and the re-tier workflow has no step that says 'now move the pin'.

records.subject: fix(sd-data): two alf reads ordered by created_at and never returned it -- give the caller the column it is ordered by
records.summary: api/sd-data.js: the alf_mar and alf_incidents list reads ordered by created_at and did not SELECT it, so the client received rows in a server-defined order with no way to verify or re-derive that order. Both client reads are hydrates that merge server rows into a persisted local array in arrival order, so the ordering became the order on disk while the column explaining it was dropped in transit.

injection.subject: fix(sairncare): six append-only trail reads had no order= clause -- not three, and unordered is not insertion order

records.citation_note: No standing rule names 'a query ordered by a column it does not return'. The nearest is the append-only read-order family that introduced the order clause, but that rule is about the ORDER being specified and this defect is about the KEY being withheld -- the rule was satisfied and the gap is beside it.
records.phase_note: The order clause was appended to an existing select during the append-only ordering pass and the select was not widened with it. A design decision to order by created_at is correct; not returning it is an omission in carrying that decision out.

contributing_factors.factor: The order clause and the select list are two halves of one query and nothing required them to agree. `&order=created_at.desc` was appended to a select that did not carry the column, and the query is valid SQL either way -- PostgREST will order by a column it does not return.
contributing_factors.action: created_at is now selected AND mapped onto the record on both reads, so the key the rows are ordered by travels with them.

contributing_factors.factor: IT IS INVISIBLE FROM THE SOURCE. The line shows an order clause and reads as complete; only the RETURNED ROWS show the column is absent. Every review of this change, including the one that approved it, read the query.
contributing_factors.action: Found by a live read-back against the deployed endpoint with real credentials, which is the method that surfaced it. Recorded so the next reviewer of an order= clause asks what the caller actually receives rather than what the query says.

contributing_factors.factor: The two affected reads are HYDRATES, not display lists -- they merge server rows into a persisted local array in arrival order and write it back. So the missing column was not merely a cosmetic omission: the server's ordering became the order on disk while the field explaining it was dropped in transit.
contributing_factors.action: Fixed on exactly the two reads with that shape. The other four trails already select the column they order by and were deliberately left alone rather than swept.

contributing_factors.factor: The sabotage arms guarding this area anchored on a hand-copied literal of the alf_mar query, so a correct change to that query broke three of them. They failed loudly about the ANCHOR rather than passing, which is the harness working -- but it is the fifth recorded instance of an arm typing a value beside the thing it is meant to watch.
contributing_factors.action: The anchors are derived from api/sd-data.js and asserted unique; arm 4's select+order argument and arm 6's order-stripped variant are computed from the matched line instead of typed again. Driven to failure by planting a second identical read.

records.recurrence_open: Only the six SAIRNcare trails were examined. Every other read on this platform that carries an order= clause is unchecked against the same question -- does the caller receive the column it is ordered by -- and the answer is invisible from the source, so a grep cannot settle it. No sweep was run.

records.subject: fix(nhi): the register runs again -- and the refusal that blocked it had surfaced a procedure that was wrong for six days
records.summary: tools/nhi_register.py REFUSED TO RUN over two unattributed credentials, so item 61's non-human-identity figures could not be re-derived at all -- a could-not-run, not a pass. Neither attribution was bookkeeping. SD_AUTH_SECRET_PREVIOUS belongs to the session-signing identity, and it FALSIFIES THAT ENTRY'S OWN PROCEDURE: the compromise text ended 'AN OVERLAP WINDOW -- accept two secrets during a changeover -- would remove that dilemma and IS A BUILD, NOT A PROCEDURE. DRAFTED 2026-09-15.' That build landed 2026-09-17 at api/_lib/auth.js:365, which accepts SD_AUTH_SECRET_PREVIOUS on verify and never signs with it -- so a rotation had not logged everyone out for six days, and the dilemma the entry posed to a human handling an incident (a certain universal logout against an uncertain compromise) was already gone. The stale claim was repeated in THREE fields of the same entry: scope, rotation and compromise. SD_ENCRYPTION_KEY is a separate identity that nothing had registered: it was split out of SD_AUTH_SECRET on 2026-09-17 precisely so a signing-key leak would stop also decrypting secrets at rest, and it is the AES-256-GCM key for attorney MFA/TOTP secrets and a stored Stedi API key. It had no owner, no rotation entry and no compromise procedure. Both were surfaced by the refusal rather than by anybody reading the register.

injection.subject: docs(sairnfreedom): the last two tips register items -- one answered, one researched into a different shape, and the register was carrying TWO tests under one word

records.citation_note: 2.3 is 'a fact with a tense needs a read, and a number needs a single source'. This is the first half exactly: DRAFTED 2026-09-15 was true when written and false two days later, and nothing re-read it. Clean citation.

contributing_factors.factor: The session-signing entry's compromise procedure ended 'AN OVERLAP WINDOW ... would remove that dilemma and IS A BUILD, NOT A PROCEDURE. DRAFTED 2026-09-15.' That build landed 2026-09-17 in api/_lib/auth.js:365, and the entry still described the pre-build world for six days. The same stale claim was repeated in THREE fields of the same entry -- scope, rotation and compromise.
contributing_factors.action: all three fields corrected, each stating what it previously said rather than quietly replacing it

contributing_factors.factor: SD_ENCRYPTION_KEY was split out of SD_AUTH_SECRET on 2026-09-17 so a session-signing leak would stop also decrypting secrets at rest. The split happened in code and nothing added the new identity to the register, so a credential protecting attorney MFA secrets and a Stedi API key had no owner, no rotation entry and no compromise procedure.
contributing_factors.action: added as its own identity with scope, rotation history and a compromise entry that states there is no revoke

contributing_factors.factor: BOTH were found by the register REFUSING TO RUN rather than by anybody reading it. The refusal on a blank owner is what made an unattributed credential impossible to ignore -- and it also blocked item 61's figures entirely, so the same guard that surfaced the problem also stopped the inventory being re-derived.
contributing_factors.action: the refusal is unchanged and is the reason this was found; recorded so it is not later softened into a warning

contributing_factors.factor: Nothing connects a code change that adds or splits a credential to the identity register. api/_lib/auth.js grew SD_AUTH_SECRET_PREVIOUS and SD_ENCRYPTION_KEY with no step that asks whether an identity entry is owed, so the register only learns about them when secrets_inventory next classifies them and the refusal fires.
contributing_factors.action: no gate ties a new process.env credential read to an identity entry; the refusal catches it eventually but only on the next run, and it is named here rather than assumed covered

records.recurrence_open: NOTHING TIES A CODE CHANGE THAT ADDS OR SPLITS A CREDENTIAL TO THE IDENTITY REGISTER. api/_lib/auth.js grew both of these with no step asking whether an entry was owed; the register only learns when secrets_inventory next classifies them and the refusal fires, which is eventual rather than immediate. AND THE SAME CLASS IS PROBABLY LIVE ELSEWHERE: this entry carried the same stale sentence in three of its own fields, and nothing checks an identity's fields against each other or against the code they describe. 17 of 23 identities still carry no compromise trigger and 23 of 23 no attested rotation date, so most entries have less text to go stale -- that is not reassurance, it is the same gap earlier.

records.subject: fix(auth): all seventeen auth endpoints took a licence for ANY app -- a StoneDesk key got 200 from SAIRNvet, and check_license is the gate that exists to stop exactly that
records.summary: All seventeen api/*-auth.js endpoints accepted a licence key issued for a DIFFERENT app. Measured live: POST /api/sv-auth {action:check_license} with Bearer SD-AUDIT-2026 (a StoneDesk licence) returned 200 {ok:true,active:true,app_id:'stonedesk'} -- SAIRNvet's own endpoint admitting a StoneDesk key and echoing the foreign app back. Each file checked lic.valid and lic.active; none compared lic.app_id to its own APP. NOT A DATA BREACH, and saying so is part of the record: api/sd-data.js:661 gates on the verified lic.app_id, so a foreign licence reaches no rows. What it does not gate is a credential row being written into another app's *_employee_auth under a foreign licence's hash, because that write never goes through sd-data.js. The reason this is a defect rather than a tidy-up is the call site's own comment: sairnvet.html:2967 says check_license runs BEFORE the key is stored precisely so 'a bad licence key gets misattributed later' cannot happen, and calls that misattribution 'the reason check_license exists at all'. It answered the exact question it was built to answer, wrongly. Fixed centrally: validateLicenseKey takes an optional expectedApp and returns a three-state app_scope, and only an explicit 'mismatch' refuses -- an unattributable licence is admitted deliberately, matching the 'cannot attribute -> cannot judge' posture api/_resources/index.js already wrote down, because refusing one would lock out real customers nobody can enumerate.

injection.unknown_reason: There is no single injecting commit. The shape was present in the FIRST auth endpoint and copied verbatim into sixteen more over several months; naming any one of them would be picking a scapegoat out of a series. What is datable is when it became reachable-and-wrong rather than merely unasked: 2026-09-05, when the data-layer boundary landed and lic.app_id started meaning something.

records.citation_note: 1.1 is about a check that cannot fail. This one could fail, on valid and on active -- it simply never asked the question its own call site says it exists to ask, so it passed a wrong-app key with full marks. Adjacent rather than exact; cited as arguable rather than clean.

contributing_factors.factor: Every api/*-auth.js validated lic.valid and lic.active and none compared the licence's own app_id to the app it was talking to. The licence layer answered 'is this a real, live key' and was read as though it had answered 'is this key for me'.
contributing_factors.action: validateLicenseKey takes an optional expectedApp and returns app_scope; every endpoint refuses an explicit mismatch with 403 LICENSE_WRONG_APP

contributing_factors.factor: The app boundary WAS built, correctly, at the data layer (sd-data.js:661, on the verified lic.app_id) eighteen days earlier. Having one correct gate one layer down is what made the missing one read as covered -- the question 'can a foreign licence reach data' was asked and answered, and 'can a foreign licence be admitted at all' was not.
contributing_factors.note: no check can catch a correct guard placed one layer later than the thing it was assumed to cover; the suite's source tripwire now covers the specific case, not the general one

contributing_factors.factor: The defect is identical in seventeen files because the licence preamble was copied verbatim into each new auth endpoint. Nothing compared a new endpoint's preamble against the others, so one omission became seventeen at zero additional cost to anyone.
contributing_factors.action: api/auth-license-app-scope.test.js asserts EVERY api/*-auth.js passes a second argument AND that the app it names is one the registry knows -- a new endpoint cannot skip it silently

contributing_factors.factor: Nothing detected it for eighteen days because there was no test that presented one app's licence to another app's auth endpoint. It was found by probing whether SD-AUDIT-2026 covered all three Wave 3 apps -- a credentials question, not a security one.
contributing_factors.action: five real handlers are now driven with a foreign licence, with a control that each still admits its own and an arm that an unattributable one is still admitted

records.recurrence_open: The tripwire covers api/*-auth.js by FILENAME. An auth surface that does not match that glob -- a new endpoint named differently, or a licence check added inside a data handler -- is not covered. And no test presents a foreign licence to the twelve NON-auth endpoints that call validateLicenseKey; the data-layer boundary is believed to cover them and that belief is not re-measured here.

records.subject: fix(sd-data): the tombstones action shipped UNREACHABLE, and a live probe is what caught it
records.summary: The new 'tombstones' action on api/sd-data.js shipped UNREACHABLE. Handlers were implemented and gated for sd_customers, sd_quote_requests and the seven soft-delete SAIRNcode resources, but the action was never declared in extraActions -- and the dispatcher checks that allowlist BEFORE any resource branch runs, so every call answered 400 'action must be read or write or soft_delete'. Seven source-level arms passed the whole time.

injection.subject: feat(sd-data): tombstones -- a deletion on one device reached no other one

records.citation_note: The nearest standing rule is Guardian check 29 -- a storage-shape change must be proven with a real write against the real endpoint -- and this is the same lesson one step sideways: a new ACTION is a two-place change and only one place is in the file being edited. Check 29 names validators and schemas, not dispatcher allowlists, so it is cited as the reasoning rather than as a rule this violated.
records.phase_note: The design was right and the handler correct. What was missed is that the dispatcher carries a declaration the handler does not live next to.

contributing_factors.factor: The dispatcher checks an action allowlist built from each app's extraActions BEFORE any resource branch runs. A handler can be fully implemented, correctly gated and completely unreachable, and nothing in the file it lives in says so.
contributing_factors.action: tombstones is now declared in api/_resources/stonedesk.js and api/_resources/sairncode.js for exactly the resources whose branch implements it.

contributing_factors.factor: THE SOURCE-LEVEL SUITE CANNOT SEE IT. Seven arms asserted the query predicate, the answer shape, the provisioned third state and the gate -- every one correct, every one green, while nothing could call the code they described. A suite that reads the handler cannot exercise the dispatcher in front of it.
contributing_factors.action: Two arms added that check the DECLARATION rather than the handler: one asserts tombstones is declared for exactly the soft-delete resources in both directions, the other that every implemented handler has a matching entry. The second is named for the lesson.

contributing_factors.factor: It was found by a LIVE PROBE against the deployed endpoint with a real licence key, immediately after the push. Nothing else in the workflow would have found it -- node --check passes, the arms pass, and the client that would have exercised it does not exist yet.
contributing_factors.action: Recorded as the reason Guardian check 29 exists: a new action on a dispatcher is a two-place change, and only one of the two places is in the file being edited.

contributing_factors.factor: The first version also carried a NO_TOMBSTONES refusal for hard-deleting resources. Once the action is declared only where a tombstone can exist, that branch became unreachable -- code that reads like a control and can never run.
contributing_factors.action: Removed rather than kept. The allowlist answers those callers first and names the verbs the resource actually has, which is the more useful refusal and needs no code to say it.

records.recurrence_open: Nothing sweeps for implemented-but-undeclared actions. Any future extraAction added to a resource branch without a registry entry fails the same way, silently, and a source-level suite will pass over it. No checker was written for this shape.

records.subject: fix(sairnvet): the Revenue MTD fold -- and the defect it was dispatched as is NOT the defect it had
records.summary: SAIRNvet's Revenue MTD KPI folded `s + (b.rate || 0) * days` across every booking in the month. Dispatched as the same uncoerced-fold defect fixed in stonedesk.html the same day, and it is NOT that class: `*` has no string overload, so the multiplication coerces before the addition sees the value. Driven, rates of "500" and "250" over 3 days give 2250, where the bare fold gives the string "0500250". WHAT WAS REAL IS SMALLER: the multiplication rescues a numeric STRING and not a junk value. "abc" * 3 is NaN, one NaN poisons the whole reduce, and the KPI rendered "$NaN" -- every other booking's revenue vanishing with it, which is a worse outcome than a single wrong row. Wrapped in Number(x) || 0 so one bad row costs that row. sairnvet.html::b.rate was in truthy_sum_baseline.json's grandfathered map carrying the recorded reason "NOT ASSESSED -- whether it is a defect depends on whether anything can put a STRING in this field", a deferral that was honest and was never resolved; it has now been assessed (a string CAN arrive, sv_boarding is server-synced) and the entry is removed. The criticality-tier row written the same morning cited the uncoerced fold as evidence of concatenation risk and was corrected in the same commit.

injection.unknown_reason: The fold predates the baseline file, which was generated 2026-09-11 and already contained this entry. Nothing dates the line itself, and picking the commit that introduced renderBoarding would name the feature rather than the defect -- the NaN behaviour was present from the first version and was never a regression.

records.citation_note: 1.1 is about a check that cannot fail. The grandfathered entry made this one unable to fail for twelve days, which is that shape via configuration rather than via a broken predicate. Cited as arguable.

contributing_factors.factor: The Revenue MTD fold read `s + (b.rate || 0) * days`. The `|| 0` guard does not coerce, but the MULTIPLICATION does -- so the string case this shape is usually reported for was never live here. What the multiplication does not rescue is a non-numeric value: "abc" * 3 is NaN, and one NaN poisons the entire reduce.
contributing_factors.action: wrapped in Number(x) || 0 so one bad row costs that row rather than the whole KPI

contributing_factors.factor: sairnvet.html::b.rate was in truthy_sum_baseline.json's grandfathered map with the recorded reason NOT ASSESSED -- explicitly deferring the question of whether a string could reach the field. The deferral was honest and it was never resolved, so the checker reported CLEAN over it for twelve days.
contributing_factors.action: assessed and removed by name, 46 to 45; a string CAN reach it because sv_boarding is server-synced, and it is harmless here for a reason now written down

contributing_factors.factor: IT WAS DISPATCHED AS THE WRONG DEFECT CLASS, and accepting that framing would have produced a fix with a false rationale attached. The dispatch called it the same class as the StoneDesk tax folds; driving it showed 2250 where the concatenation class gives "0500250".
contributing_factors.action: measured before changing anything, and the tier row that carried the wrong rationale was corrected in the same commit rather than left standing

contributing_factors.factor: truthy_sum_check.py reports `+ (x || 0) * y` even though its own docstring states multiplication is safe. That is deliberate -- it is a HAZARD reporter, not a defect detector -- but it means a report from it cannot be read as a defect without driving the expression.
contributing_factors.note: narrowing it to exclude a following `*` would hide the case where somebody later removes the multiplication; the over-report is the safe direction and the tool already says so

records.recurrence_open: 45 grandfathered entries remain and most carry the same NOT ASSESSED wording this one did -- a deferral nobody has returned to. This is the second in one day to turn out to matter (stonedesk.html::b.amt and ::e.tax were the first), and neither was found by looking at the list. Nothing schedules a review of it. AND THE FOLD SHAPE REMAINS AMBIGUOUS TO THE TOOL: truthy_sum_check.py reports `+ (x || 0) * y` although its own docstring says multiplication is safe, so a report from it still cannot be read as a defect without driving the expression. That is deliberate and the safe direction, but it means the remaining 45 cannot be triaged from the report alone.

records.subject: fix(roofing): an inherited Object.prototype name was passing the role gate
records.summary: api/rf-auth.js built MANAGEMENT_ROLES and BROAD_READ_ROLES as plain object literals, so every key on Object.prototype indexed truthy: seesAllRows({role:'constructor'}) returned true, reproduced live. A session carrying an inherited name passed the role half of every SAIRNroofing gate -- seesAllRows, ownsRow, and the ~40 sites in api/sd-data.js that index those maps directly -- granting cross-assignee read and write on rf_claims and rf_claim_photos, both Tier A. It was inert only because a SEPARATE array-based allowlist at provisioning (RF_ROLES.indexOf) refuses an unknown role, which is distant code the gate was silently depending on rather than a property of the check itself. Second defect in the same finding: the rf_claims write branch never stripped the caller's own assigned_employee_id from the stored data blob, inert only because the read branch's Object.assign happens to overlay the real column last.

injection.subject: feat(sairnroofing): Phase 1 credential-lifecycle auth backend, roles confirmed

records.citation_note: No standing rule on this platform names "a JS object literal used as a membership set inherits Object.prototype, so an inherited name indexes truthy". The closest are the cross-domain disciplines' warning about a guard that is safe only because of distant code, and the silent-failure sweep -- neither is about the prototype chain, and citing either would be a stretch dressed as a citation. Recorded as not-citable so the gap is visible: this is a candidate for a new rule, since the same plain-literal shape is present in nine other api/*.js role maps.
records.phase_note: Injected at the moment the role maps were first written as object literals in b9b15bfb (SAIRNroofing Phase 1 auth backend). The shape is a design choice about how a membership set is represented, not a coding slip: the literal is correct-looking, matches eight other apps, and only fails on names it never intended to accept.

contributing_factors.factor: A JS object literal used as a membership set inherits every key on Object.prototype, so MANAGEMENT_ROLES['constructor'] is truthy. The set was correct about every name it meant to accept and silent about nine it never considered.
contributing_factors.action: Both maps are now built by roleSet() with a null prototype, which fixes the ~40 direct-index call sites in api/sd-data.js without editing any of them. seesAllRows also goes through hasRole(), an own-property check, so the gate holds even if a map is rebuilt as a literal.

contributing_factors.factor: The defect was inert only because of a separate, array-based allowlist in a different branch of a different function (RF_ROLES.indexOf at provisioning). Nothing at the gate said so, and nothing at the allowlist said the gate depended on it.
contributing_factors.action: The gate no longer depends on it: an inherited name is refused at the gate itself, with the coupling and why it is not relied on written into the code at the role maps.

contributing_factors.factor: Every behavioural arm in the existing suite drove real role names, so the suite could not have caught this and did not claim to. The gap was in which INPUTS were considered a role, not in the predicate's logic.
contributing_factors.action: Eight arms added over nine inherited names covering both helpers, direct indexing of the exported maps, and the null prototype itself -- with a negative control asserting a plain literal of the same roles still leaks, so the arms cannot pass by testing nothing. Two sabotage mutations (arms 8 and 9) plant both defects back and are refused.

contributing_factors.factor: The same plain-literal shape was copied into nine other api/*.js role maps (accounting, ledger, alf, bld, dnt, dnt-bi, leg, mech, and rf-auth's own KNOWN_CERTIFICATION_KEYS). A pattern propagated by copy was never re-qualified at each destination.
contributing_factors.action: Reported to Michael as a separate finding with the nine files named, rather than folded into this fix. Deliberately NOT swept here: byte-identical is not safe-in-context, so each destination needs its own role vocabulary and blast radius re-qualified, which is a decision to schedule and not a diff to ride along with a Tier A fix.

contributing_factors.factor: The rf_claims write built its stored blob from the caller's whole payload and removed fields by an explicit delete list, so any field added to the payload is stored unless somebody remembers to add it. assigned_employee_id was never on the list.
contributing_factors.action: assigned_employee_id is stripped on the write, where the guarantee belongs, rather than relying on the read branch's Object.assign ordering. A suite arm asserts the delete exists AND that it precedes the POST.

records.recurrence_open: The actions close this app's role maps and this app's claim write. They do NOT close the nine other api/*.js files carrying the identical plain-literal shape -- each is inert or not for its own reasons and none has been checked. They also do not close the delete-list shape generally: every resource whose stored blob is built from the caller's payload minus an explicit list has the same "a new field is stored unless somebody remembers" property, and no check counts those. Nothing on this platform currently detects either shape; both were found by reading, and a second reader is not a control.

records.subject: fix(service-role-gate): the report truncated 226 resources to 3 in silence, and two claims about it were stale
records.summary: tools/service_role_tier_a_gate_check.py printed each file's Tier A resource list truncated to three names with nothing to say it had truncated. On api/sd-data.js that is 3 of 226, so the report line read "alf_billing, alf_claim_routes, alf_clients" and a reader would take the single largest Tier A surface on the platform for a file that barely touches Tier A data. THE CLASSIFICATION WAS NEVER WRONG -- only the reporting layer was, which is the more dangerous half: a wrong verdict gets argued with, a truthful verdict under a misleading summary gets believed. Same shape as the fabrication rule this platform already holds, where blanking a KPI value while leaving "4 in progress" beside it is worse than not blanking it at all. TWO STALE CLAIMS ABOUT THE SAME TOOL WERE FIXED WITH IT: the registry entry and the generated TOOLING-INVENTORY row both said "It reports CLEAN today" when it names three UNGATED findings and one COULD NOT RUN and exits 2 permanently; and api/bridge.js's push comment still argued that requiring a licence key "would just trade a 404 for a 401, not fix anything live", an argument written while `pull` existed and invalidated when `pull` was removed on 2026-09-17 for a raw-licence-key exposure that applies equally to the write side.

injection.unknown_reason: The truncation was present from the tool's first version on 2026-09-15 and no commit introduced it. The two stale claims each became false when something ELSE changed -- the tool got more honest, and pull was removed from bridge.js -- so neither has an injection point either.

records.citation_note: No standing rule names a REPORT that truncates silently while its classification stays correct. The nearest are the fabrication discipline (a blanked KPI with a surviving sub-label) and Guardian's no-silent-caps line in the coverage-disclosure section; neither is written as a rule about a checker's own output. Closest match recorded rather than forced.
records.phase_note: Not introduced in a phase. A cap that was reasonable when the largest file held a handful of Tier A resources became misleading as api/sd-data.js grew to 226.
records.factors_unknown_reason: Not yet worked through by an independent session. Named in the commit: a cap with no disclosure, a caveat that went stale because its subject improved, and an argument whose premise was removed a week later.

records.subject: fix(bridge): my own correction to this comment was wrong, and it overstated an exposure
records.summary: A CORRECTION TO A STALE COMMENT WAS ITSELF WRONG, AND IT OVERSTATED A SECURITY EXPOSURE. api/bridge.js's header paragraph for the `push` action argued that requiring a licence key "would just trade a 404 for a 401, not fix anything live" -- written while the `pull` action still existed, and left behind when `pull` was removed on 2026-09-17. While fixing that staleness I wrote that the exposure was still live: that anyone holding a shop's licence key could still overwrite its whole {jobs, invoices, employees} blob because nothing authenticated the caller. BOTH HALVES WERE FALSE. handlePush has required a licence since 2026-09-17 -- 401 NO_LICENCE with no Authorization header, a real validateLicenseKey call, 503 LICENCE_UNCHECKED failing CLOSED if the licence store cannot answer, and 403 BAD_LICENCE otherwise -- and the upsert key is `license_hash`, renamed and rehashed in place by sql/bridge_data_rekey_2026-09-18.sql, so the raw licence key is no longer stored at all. THE CAUSE IS THE SAME ONE THE HEADER ITSELF SUFFERS FROM: I read the file's header and not the handler sixty lines below it, which is precisely the mistake I was correcting, committed by the person correcting it. It was caught within the hour and not by me -- the push gate's pre-auth oracle scan printed this file's own `401 NO_LICENCE` string back on the way out. A WRONG SECURITY CLAIM IS WORSE THAN THE STALE ONE IT REPLACED: the stale version understated the protection and would have prompted somebody to go and look, while this one overstated the exposure and would have sent them to fix something already fixed. The error is recorded in the comment rather than quietly overwritten, so the next reader can tell a corrected claim from an original one.

injection.subject: fix(service-role-gate): the report truncated 226 resources to 3 in silence, and two claims about it were stale

records.citation_note: PR 1.5 is the verify-before-you-report rule: a status claim is a claim, not a fact, until checked against real current state. That is exactly what failed -- the claim was checked against the file's HEADER rather than against the handler, and a header is a document about the code, not the code.
records.phase_note: Injected while fixing a different and real staleness in the same comment block, in the same commit as three correct fixes. The lag from injection to detection was under an hour.
records.factors_unknown_reason: Not yet worked through independently. The shape is named in the commit: correcting a stale header BY reading the header, when the fact lives in the handler sixty lines below.

records.subject: fix(probe): the sabotage control has been mutating the WRONG SC query, and reporting it as 24 broken arms
records.summary: tests/run_cross_tenant_dispatchers_sabotage_probe.py locates each branch by its opener and DERIVES the read line as "the first tenant filter at or below it, within 90 lines" -- deliberately, so a typed line number cannot rot. On 2026-09-23 a `tombstones` action with its own license_hash-filtered query was added to the SAIRNcode branch and landed BETWEEN `if (isScResource) {` (line 13341) and the generic list read (13444). The first filter below the opener became the tombstones query at +81, which no isolation arm drives, while the read the control exists for sits at +103 -- past the tombstones line AND past the 90-line window. So the SC_RESOURCES mutation removed a tenant filter nothing tested and the control reported `24 arm(s) the mutation should have turned red stayed green`, which reads as twenty-four broken cross-tenant arms on SAIRNcode's Tier A billing resources. The arms are correct -- removing license_hash from 13444 by hand turns exactly those 24 red. The control did not fail silently; it failed LOUDLY ABOUT THE WRONG THING, which this file's own header names as the worse outcome, and for a day the only sabotage control over 23 Tier A sc_ resources was verifying nothing.

injection.unknown_reason: The tombstones action that landed between the opener and the read is on 2026-09-23 and is identifiable, but the defect is in the PROBE's derivation rule, which was correct when written -- so naming the feature commit as the injection would credit the wrong change. The rule's own commit is the honest candidate and I did not establish which it is.

contributing_factors.factor: THE DERIVATION RULE ASSUMED ONE FILTERED QUERY PER BRANCH. `first tenant filter below the opener` is correct exactly while a branch has one such query. Nothing enforced that assumption and nothing stated it: the rule was chosen to avoid a typed line number rotting, and it replaced one kind of rot with a quieter one -- an anchor that still matches, on the wrong line.
contributing_factors.action: A branch row may now carry a read MARKER -- a substring the read line must also contain -- so a branch with several filtered queries says which one is its read. SC's is `scSoftFilter`. A marker that matches nothing is a MISS and never falls back to proximity.

contributing_factors.factor: A FEATURE LANDED INSIDE A BRANCH A CONTROL WAS ANCHORED ON, and there is no reason the author would have known. The tombstones commit added an action to api/sd-data.js; the control lives in tests/ and names no line numbers, so nothing connected the two. The window was documented as 90 with the reason 'SC is the widest real gap at 68 lines' -- a measured number that quietly became 103.
contributing_factors.action: The window is now 160 with the measurement and the date beside it, so the next reader can see when it was last checked rather than inferring it still holds. What is NOT built is anything that re-measures it; that is named in the recurrence note rather than claimed.

contributing_factors.factor: IT WAS ONLY FOUND BECAUSE A REVIEW OBLIGATION ASKED FOR IT BY NAME. hank's own point (5) said to re-run the control rather than trust its summary, having been bitten once already by an anchor hitting a byte-identical branch. Nothing runs this probe automatically, so without that sentence the MISS would have sat until somebody happened to run it.
contributing_factors.note: Promoting a ~10-minute sabotage probe into the push gate is a real cost decision for its owner, not a change to make inside a review discharge. Recorded so the choice is visible.

records.recurrence_open: THE MARKER IS ON ONE ROW. Fourteen other branches still locate their read by proximity alone, and any one of them acquires this defect the moment a second filtered query is added above its read -- which is exactly what happened here, from an unrelated feature commit. Nothing measures how close any of them is to its window, and the count of branches with more than one license_hash-filtered query is UNMEASURED rather than one. Also open: READ_WINDOW is now 160 because 103 was measured today, and nothing re-measures it -- the previous number was 90 with '68 lines' written beside it and that sentence was true when written. And the probe is run by hand; nothing schedules it, so the gap between a control going blind and anybody noticing is however long it takes for somebody to be told to run it.

records.subject: fix(sairnfreedom): an executed signature was reachable on the licence key alone -- the second half of a pair closed by halves
records.summary: sf_signatures reached api/sd-data.js with no session gate: the SF_RESOURCES read and write branches dispatched on the licence hash alone, and the licence key is shipped to the browser and readable by anyone who can open the app. The row is {docId, docTitle, version, hash, signer, typed, signed} -- a named person, their typed signature, and the governance document it binds them to, with a hash of the text they signed. It is not a fact ABOUT a person but a reusable instrument that can be lifted off one document and re-applied to another, which is why it is sharper than the identity rows gated beside it. Named alongside sf_members in the 2026-09-22 finding; sf_members was closed that day and this one was left with the words 'the open-work row stays open'. Reachability was demonstrated live on 2026-09-22 -- 200 provisioned:true with no session token, against a control where sf_ledger answered 403 -- and exfiltration was NOT: every probe returned zero rows on that tenant.

injection.subject: feat(sairnvet,sairnfreedom): the two apps that kept everything on one device now back it up -- 76 collections, SQL NOT RUN

records.citation_note: docs/SAIRN-PROCESS-RULES.md is about how this team works -- checks, claims, pushes, standing documents. It has no section naming 'a Tier A resource authorised by a licence key alone', which is a product-security shape rather than a process one. The rule this DOES violate is written in api/sd-data.js's own gate comment and in docs/CRITICALITY-TIERS.md, neither of which is a citable section. Recording not-citable rather than stretching PR 1.11, which is about a check failing closed when a dependency is absent and is not this.

contributing_factors.factor: SAIRNfreedom's 35 resources reached api/sd-data.js in one commit with no session gate of any kind -- the app had no per-employee auth, so the licence key was the whole boundary by construction and nothing in the change had to argue for it per resource
contributing_factors.action: Employee auth landed 2026-09-21 (schema, ROLES_BY_APP, api/sf-auth.js, X-SD-Auth in the client), which is what made a per-resource gate possible at all.

contributing_factors.factor: The deferral comment described the ungated remainder as 'a duty roster or a bottle count'. That description does not cover a named person's executed signature, so anyone reading it to decide was deciding about the wrong set
contributing_factors.action: Replaced 2026-09-22 with the actual list. This change adds sf_signatures' row shape, read out of the app rather than off the schema.

contributing_factors.factor: The finding named two resources and one batch closed one of them. The other was recorded as still open and stayed open for two days with nothing scheduled against it
contributing_factors.action: Closed. The suite arm that asserted its absence was replaced with set equality against an APPROVED list, which fails on an unapproved addition AND on a resource quietly losing its gate.

contributing_factors.factor: Two suites guarding this gate were RED on origin/main from 2026-09-22 and nobody noticed: api/sf-session-gate.test.js asserted sf_members was ungated on the day it was gated, and api/sd-data-session-gate.test.js held a pair count of 23 against a table of 55 plus a coverage map naming 3 of 15 sf_ resources
contributing_factors.action: Both repaired. The sf_ coverage half is now a derived loop driving every gated sf_ resource through the real dispatcher, with the coverage arm verifying that loop exists rather than trusting a hand-written map.

contributing_factors.factor: The sabotage probe's widening mutation planted sf_members and sf_signatures, both of which became approved -- so the planted defect was a no-op and the probe reported the suite as silent when the suite was correct
contributing_factors.action: Mutation 6 now widens to sf_officers and sf_tickets; mutation 7 reopens sf_signatures so the closure has an arm holding it.

records.recurrence_open: NOTHING STOPS THE NEXT RESOURCE BEING GATED BY HALVES. The approved list is set equality now, so a gate cannot widen or narrow silently -- but nothing schedules the DECISION for the resources still ungated, and 'nobody has made that call' is indistinguishable from 'the call was made and was no'. Separately, the two suites that went red for two days went red because a change landed that tripped them and was pushed anyway; no gate refuses a push that leaves a named guard suite failing, which is the general form of this and is not closed here.

records.subject: fix(probe): A8 of the rollup-list review probe has been CRASHING, not passing
records.summary: tests/criticality_rollup_list_review_probe.py arm A8 dropped a name from the StoneDesk rollup cell with SD.replace('`name`, ', '', 1) -- name, comma, space -- which is how every name in that cell is written EXCEPT THE LAST ONE. `sd_crm` is the first exactly-once name today and it is the final element, so the replace planted nothing, drive()'s bytes-changed guard fired, and the probe died with an AssertionError partway through A8. Every arm after it never ran. Confirmed red at origin/main and unrelated to the session that found it. The probe's own subject is finding stale anchors in OTHER probes' arms, and it had the same defect in its own -- the fourth time this exact anchor shape has bitten on this register, after arm 9 of run_criticality_tier_probe.py was repaired for the same reason on the same name on 2026-09-23.

injection.unknown_reason: The arm was written with this spelling; which edit to the StoneDesk rollup cell made sd_crm the final element -- and so turned a working anchor into a dead one -- is not established here, and guessing a sha would be a lag with a hash on it.

contributing_factors.factor: THE ANCHOR ENCODED A POSITION IT DID NOT CHECK. `name`, with a trailing comma and space is only how a NON-FINAL list element is written. The arm derived WHICH name to drop from the fixture -- correctly, and that is the discipline the file's own header preaches -- but then hardcoded a spelling that assumes where in the list that name sits. Deriving the value and hardcoding the shape around it is half the rule.
contributing_factors.action: Three spellings tried in order -- mid-list, last-in-list, alone -- plus an assert that the name is actually absent afterwards. The identical repair hank made to arm 9 on 2026-09-23.

contributing_factors.factor: THE SAME REPAIR WAS MADE NEXT DOOR AND NOT PROPAGATED. Arm 9 of run_criticality_tier_probe.py had this exact defect, on this exact name, and was fixed on 2026-09-23. Nothing looked for the pattern anywhere else, and this file -- whose entire purpose is reviewing those arms -- carried a copy.
contributing_factors.action: Recorded here so the pair is findable. A grep for the `name`, spelling across tests/ is cheap and has not been run; it is named rather than claimed.

contributing_factors.factor: A REPORT-ONLY PROBE THAT DIES IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ONE WITH NOTHING TO SAY, to anybody not reading its last line. This probe never fails a push by design, so a traceback partway through costs nothing visible: the arms after A8 simply did not run and no gate anywhere noticed.
contributing_factors.note: The honest fix is that a report-only probe should still exit non-zero when it CRASHED, as opposed to when it merely found things -- could-not-run is a third state, PR 1.11. That is a change to the probe's exit contract and to whatever reads it, and it belongs to its own claim rather than to a one-line anchor repair.

records.recurrence_open: THE PATTERN IS NOT SWEPT. This is the fourth instance of the same anchor shape on this one register and the second in two days; nothing has grepped tests/ for the `name`, spelling, and the count of remaining instances is UNMEASURED rather than zero. Also open, and larger: a report-only probe that CRASHES still exits 0 here, so the arms after the crash silently do not run and nothing distinguishes that from a clean report -- the could-not-tell-folded-into-a-pass shape, in a file whose job is to catch it in others. Neither is closed by this fix.

records.subject: fix(sairnlaw): the comment above law_clients made three claims and all three had gone false
records.summary: The comment block immediately above the law_clients branch in api/sd-data.js asserted three facts and all three had gone false, two of them about authentication: "No verifySessionToken/role check on any of these three resources" (law_clients, law_matters and law_deadlines entered SD_SESSION_GATED for read and write on 2026-09-22, with SD_GATE_APP pinning each to 'sairnlaw'), "sdnData() never sends a session token to this endpoint" (sairnlaw.html sets X-SD-Auth on every data call whenever a token exists), and "these three read routes are live but currently unreachable from the client -- zero sdnData('read',...) calls anywhere" (law_clients is a member of LAW_SYNC_RESOURCES and lawHydrateAll reads every member). The two security claims are stale in the direction that reads as an OPEN HOLE: the session check is absent from this branch because it runs centrally, so the branch genuinely looks ungated from here and the comment confirms the wrong reading rather than correcting it. It cost real work -- the cross-tenant review obligation opened 2026-09-23T09:54Z built its point (3) on claim (1) and asked a reviewer to confirm a phase-2 gap that had been closed two days earlier.

records.subject: fix(spof): the retirement disclosure went SILENT exactly when the list was growing -- and its own control arm has been red
records.summary: tools/dependency_graph.py's SPOF-register check printed its retirement disclosure ("NOTHING HAS BEEN RETIRED YET") only when net == 0 -- the live count exactly equalling the frozen baseline -- so the sentence went SILENT in every state except the one where nothing at all had happened. On 2026-09-23 the register stood at 32 components against a baseline of 11 with zero retirements in nine days, and the tool said nothing about retirement: the GROWTH suppressed the disclosure. A disclosure that disappears when the situation worsens is not a disclosure. And its control probe's arm 7e -- the ONE arm in the register section asserting rc == 0 -- has been red at HEAD, because its fixture carried no BASELINE sentence; so 7d's refusal was unverified and nothing proved the checker refuses an empty register for the stated reason rather than refusing everything. Fixed: the stall prints unconditionally with ELAPSED TIME read from the same frozen sentence as the count (an undated baseline is refused as its own problem line), and four probe arms pin the growth case, the elapsed-time text, the paired positive (a RETIRED row changes the line), and the undated refusal.

injection.unknown_reason: The net==0 gate shipped with the register check itself; identifying that commit needs the file's history walked for check_register's introduction and I did not establish it -- a guessed sha would be a lag with a hash on it.

records.citation_note: 1.1's shape -- a check that stopped checking -- is the closest fit and is a stretch in one respect: the disclosure never checked the growth case, so it is a check that NEVER STARTED for that state rather than one that stopped. The family (a green-looking output concealing an unexercised path) is the same; cited arguable for that scope difference.

contributing_factors.factor: THE CONDITION ENCODED ONE SCENARIO, NOT THE PROPERTY. `net == 0 and not retired` was written when the register had just opened and the only imaginable quiet state was 'nothing moved yet'. The property -- zero retirements should always be said out loud with how long it has been true -- was never stated, so the first state outside the author's imagination (growth) fell outside the condition.
contributing_factors.action: The disclosure is unconditional on `not retired`, carries elapsed days from the baseline date, and the paired-positive arm proves it is not printed when a retirement exists.

contributing_factors.factor: THE CONTROL THAT WOULD HAVE FORCED THE QUESTION WAS ITSELF BROKEN. Arm 7e was the section's only rc == 0 assertion and was red at HEAD on a fixture defect (no BASELINE sentence), so the whole register section of the probe had no working positive control -- and a probe whose control is red teaches its reader to stop reading exactly the section that needed reading.

contributing_factors.factor: REPORT-ONLY OUTPUT HAS NO READER OF RECORD. The stall sentence is advisory prose in a --register run; nobody's workflow breaks when it goes missing, so its absence for nine days was noticed only when a queue item said to look.
