records.subject: fix(sairncode): the PT panel had no GP rule at all -- the one missing modifier that stops a claim being adjudicated
records.summary: SAIRNcode's Physical Therapy panel had no GP rule and no GP field: the word did not appear anywhere in sairncode.html. The panel checked the 8-minute rule, the KX threshold, CQ, MPPR and the 2026 RTM windows, and every one of those was correct -- but GP is the therapy DISCIPLINE modifier, required on every always-therapy service furnished under a physical-therapy plan of care (GO for occupational therapy, GN for speech-language pathology). A therapy line submitted without one is returned as UNPROCESSABLE: the claim is not denied, it is never adjudicated at all. So the panel's headline answer on a PT session with no GP was "No blocking issues found by the checks that ran" -- literally true, and the worst practically available answer, because the missing modifier was the one that stops the submission rather than one that changes what it pays. CQ costs 15%; KX costs an appeal; this costs the whole claim.

injection.unknown_reason: Absent from the panel since it was built (Phase 5 item 11). No commit introduced the defect; the panel shipped with five correct rules and without a sixth, so there is no injection point to name.

records.citation_note: No standing rule names this shape. The nearest is the coverage-disclosure discipline -- a panel that lists what it checks must not read as checking a category it does not -- but the tooltip here was ACCURATE about everything it named ("8-minute rule, KX threshold, CQ modifier, MPPR, 2026 RTM codes"), so nothing in the app was false. The gap was an absent rule, not a wrong claim, and the specific reason it stayed absent is a name collision this platform has no rule about: "PT" already means the preventive-to-diagnostic modifier in the Modifier Routing panel, so a reader searching for therapy modifiers finds "PT" throughout the file and reads the area as covered.
records.phase_note: Not introduced in a phase -- the rule was never written. The panel's own originating brief listed the modifiers it covers and GP was not among them.
records.factors_unknown_reason: Named in the obligation opened against this commit and not yet worked through by an independent session: the 'PT' name collision with the preventive modifier, and the fact that a panel listing what it checks gives no signal about what it does not.

records.subject: fix(write-audit): the fifth false-positive class -- a call inside a comment is not a call
records.summary: tools/sync_write_result_check.py scanned transport calls written inside `//` comments as if they were real call sites. Three on the live codebase -- sairndental.html:5264, sairndesign.html:2394, sairngrounds.html:1683 -- and every one is a comment EXPLAINING a write, two of them explaining a write that had been deliberately REMOVED. They were reported as COULD NOT TELL, which is the right answer to the wrong question: there is nothing to tell because there is no call. IT COST IN THREE DIRECTIONS AND THE THIRD IS THE WORST. The write COUNT is the denominator of every figure the tool prints, and it was over by three. Three could-not-tells sat permanently unresolvable, and a third-state column that can never reach zero is one people stop reading. And a comment quoting a call it removed would be reported forever, so the honest act of writing down what you took out made the tool noisier -- a checker that penalises good documentation is one people route around. THIS IS THE FIFTH FALSE-POSITIVE CLASS found in this checker; four were already fixed (await read as a consumer, a delayed multi-line .then(), an array element inside Promise.all, and a bracket opened on an earlier line). AND THIS CODEBASE HAD ALREADY PAID FOR THIS EXACT CLASS: tools/sairn_dead_button_audit.py records 58 phantom findings on StoneDesk from scanning comments, and its fix was a real state machine rather than a regex. The lesson was written down and had not reached here.

injection.unknown_reason: Present from the tool's first version. No commit introduced it; the three comments it trips on were written independently, two of them AFTER the tool, by sessions documenting a write they had removed.

records.citation_note: The applicable rule is a repo CONVENTION rather than a numbered process rule: tools/sairn_dead_button_audit.py's header records that scanning comments cost 58 phantom findings on StoneDesk and that the fix is a real state machine, not a regex. It is not a section in SAIRN-PROCESS-RULES.md, so not-citable is the honest field value -- and the fact that a lesson this expensive lives only in one tool's header is part of why it did not reach a sibling tool solving the same problem.
records.phase_note: Not introduced in a phase. The scanner never stripped comments, and the population it trips on grows every time somebody documents a removal honestly.
records.factors_unknown_reason: Not yet worked through independently. The commit names the shape: a documented lesson living in one tool's header, never generalised, not reaching a sibling tool with the same problem.

records.subject: fix(tier-a-gate): --list's exit 1 meant 'the queue has overdue work' and was being read as 'this file is invalid'
records.summary: docs/tier-a-reviews.json named tier_a_review_gate.py --list as its merge validator, and --list exits 1 whenever ANY obligation is past its 24h deadline. tools/sairn_rebase_resolve.py refuses any merge whose validator exits non-zero, so a correct union-by-identity merge of the review ledger was refused whenever the queue happened to hold overdue work -- which is most of the time, and is not a fact about the file being merged. Two unrelated questions shared one exit code: is this file sound, and does the queue hold overdue work.

injection.subject: fix(rebase): the two JSON registers get a real 3-way merge, not a side taken

records.citation_note: No standing rule covers 'a tool's exit code means one thing to a human and another to a machine that reuses it'. The nearest family is the could-not-tell-folded-into-a-pass rule, but this is its mirror image: a clean state folded into a failure. Recorded as not-citable with the shape named rather than stretched onto a rule it does not fit.
records.phase_note: The merge policy was written naming the only mode that existed. The defect is in choosing a validator whose exit semantics were never for that purpose, not in the implementation of either tool.

contributing_factors.factor: ONE EXIT CODE CARRIED TWO QUESTIONS. --list returns 1 when any obligation is past its 24h deadline, which is correct for a person reading the queue. The merge policy pointed at it, and sairn_rebase_resolve.py treats any non-zero validator exit as 'this merge produced a file its own gate rejects'. Soundness and queue state are unrelated facts and nothing separated them.
contributing_factors.action: A second mode, --validate, answers soundness only and exits 0 or 2 -- never 1 -- so the two cannot share a code again. The merge policy names it, with the reason recorded in the policy note.

contributing_factors.factor: THE FIX THAT WOULD HAVE BEEN WRONG WAS THE OBVIOUS ONE. Changing --list to exit 0 would have unblocked every rebase and removed the only mechanical signal that an obligation is being ignored -- trading a real alarm for a convenience, on the register built specifically because a queue nobody closes is a queue people stop reading.
contributing_factors.action: --list is untouched. The new mode was added beside it and the divergence is asserted by a probe arm rather than left as a comment.

contributing_factors.factor: IT WAS INVISIBLE FROM EITHER FILE. tier_a_review_gate.py does not know it is a merge validator; sairn_rebase_resolve.py does not know what exit 1 means to the tool it runs. The coupling lives in a JSON field in a third file, and neither side reads the other.
contributing_factors.action: Recorded rather than fixed: a validator contract stated in a data file and enforced nowhere is the general shape, and the only defence added here is that --validate's exit codes are documented at its definition. No mechanism checks that a declared validator has the right exit semantics.
contributing_factors.note: Not actionable as a check, and that is a decision rather than a deferral. Nothing can mechanically test what a third-party tool's exit 1 is SUPPOSED to mean -- the semantics live in prose. What could be built is a rule that a merge validator must never exit 1, but that would be a convention imposed on tools this repo does not own. Recorded as the shape to look for when a merge_policy names a new validator.

contributing_factors.factor: MY OWN FIRST VERSION OF THE NEW VALIDATOR WAS WRONG IN THE SAME FAMILY: it typed the status vocabulary as ('open','discharged') instead of reading it out of the writers, and refused 109 of 127 real records on its first run against the live ledger. A validator that refuses the file it certifies is worse than none.
contributing_factors.action: STATUSES is derived by reading the three sites that assign a status -- _discharge()'s two callers plus --open -- and a probe arm asserts all three are accepted. Caught by driving it against the real ledger rather than a fixture.

records.recurrence_open: Every other merge_policy validator on this platform is unchecked against the same question. docs/defect-density-register.json names defect_register.py --check, which happens to be a validity check, but nothing enforces that a declared validator answers soundness rather than content. A second ledger adopting a --list-shaped validator would reproduce this exactly.

records.subject: fix(verification-plan): zero checkable items out of ten was returning EXIT 0
records.summary: tools/verification_plan_staleness_check.py returned EXIT 0 when the plan it read had item lines and NOT ONE verify marker: nothing was measured, it printed "drift found 0", and main() returned 0. A caller reading the exit code -- a push gate, a cron, another tool -- could not distinguish "checked ten items and they all agree" from "could check none of them". The file's own header refuses exactly that shape one paragraph above the bug ("a staleness checker that reports a clean plan it never opened is the defect it exists to prevent"), and the probe already had an arm for the neighbouring case (a plan with zero item LINES is exit 2) which never reached this one. Found by running the tool against its real subject the day that subject was first committed; before that the tool had only ever been run against synthetic fixtures that all carried markers.

injection.unknown_reason: The tool was authored in a commit the rebase has since rewritten more than once; naming a sha that may not be reachable would be worse than saying so. It was injected when the tool was first written, 2026-09-24, in the same session.

records.citation_note: PR §1.11 is the closest standing rule and it is about a check that depends on an ABSENT TOOL, which is not this. This is a check whose subject is PRESENT and unmeasurable, reporting a pass. The family is the same -- "could not run" is a third state and is never folded into "passed" -- so it is cited rather than recorded as uncitable.
records.phase_note: The third state was implemented for the absent-plan shape and for a zero-item plan, and the items-present-none-checkable shape was simply not considered. The probe's arm for the neighbouring case shows the author was thinking about it and stopped one shape short.

contributing_factors.factor: The could-not-tell third state was implemented for one shape (no plan file, or a plan with zero item lines) and not for the neighbouring one (items present, none carrying a verify marker). The printed output named UNVERIFIABLE as 'a THIRD state, not clean' while the exit code folded it into clean.
contributing_factors.action: Zero checkable items out of a non-zero number of items is now exit 2 with the reason printed. The verdict is computed in one function used by both the human and the --json path, so the two cannot diverge on what counts as could-not-tell.

contributing_factors.factor: A PARTIAL measurement had no stated meaning either. Making the tool strict enough to catch the bug would have made every real plan permanently could-not-tell, which is the opposite failure and just as useless.
contributing_factors.action: Partial stays exit 0 when the checkable items agree, and now always prints how many were NOT measured so the zero cannot be read against the wrong denominator. Arm 7b is the paired control that refuses the over-strict implementation.

contributing_factors.factor: The tool had never been run against its real subject, because the subject was chat's own planning document and was not repo-tracked. Every probe arm drove a synthetic plan, and every synthetic plan happened to carry verify markers -- so the branch where none does was never executed.
contributing_factors.action: The plan is now committed and arm 1b reads it. The probe's closing note states plainly which branch the real plan exercises and that the rest are fixtures, so the limit is declared rather than discovered.

contributing_factors.factor: The probe's arm 1 drove the absent-plan case by running the tool bare. That stopped being the absent case the moment the plan was committed, and TWO of its three assertions kept passing while testing something else -- exit 2 for an unrelated reason, and the path named because it was the path it OPENED rather than the path it looked for.
contributing_factors.action: Absence is now driven against a copy of the tool in a throwaway tree with no plan in it, which reaches the real search-miss branch. The tool resolves its repo root from its own __file__, so this is the only way to reach that branch while the plan exists, and the arm says so.

records.recurrence_open: The actions close the exit-code semantics of this one tool. They do NOT close the class: no check on this platform asks whether a tool's exit 0 means "measured and clean" or "measured nothing". The register itself, the tier-A gate and the generators each answer this differently and correctly, but by hand, and nothing enumerates the tools that do not. They also do not close the plan's own unverifiability -- the committed plan carries zero verify markers, so the tool will answer exit 2 COULD NOT TELL until somebody marks items in it, and nothing schedules that.

records.subject: fix(platform): all 48 role membership sets get a null prototype, not just roofing
records.summary: api/_lib/auth.js built every role membership set as a plain object literal, and so did 48 sites across 19 files that follow the same convention: MANAGEMENT_ROLES, BROAD_READ_ROLES, AUTHENTICATED_ROLES, ALERT_ROLES, PRESCRIBER_ROLES, AI_COC_REVIEW_ROLES, FINANCIAL_ROLES, 25 function-local maps in api/sd-data.js, plus ROLES_BY_APP and AUTH_TABLE_BY_APP. A plain literal inherits Object.prototype, so MAP['constructor'] indexes truthy and an inherited name reads as a role at every `MAP[session.role]` gate on the platform -- money (accounting, ledger, trust reconciliation), clinical (MAR, incidents, credentials, veterinary prescribing), patient and employee PII, and statutory governance. ALL 48 WERE INERT FOR ONE DISTANT REASON, not for 48 local ones: verifySessionToken() re-validates payload.role against ROLES_BY_APP on every verification, so no session carrying an inherited name reached any gate. That is a single function 48 authorisation gates silently depended on, with nothing at either end saying so; narrowing its vocabulary or adding one caller that mints a session another way would open all 48 at once. Separately, ROLES_BY_APP is itself indexed by payload.app inside that function, where the plain literal made ROLES_BY_APP['constructor'] a truthy function that then threw on .indexOf -- a 500 where a null session was intended.

injection.unknown_reason: The convention predates the register and spread across 19 files over months; no single commit introduced it, and naming one would be a guess dressed as a citation.

records.citation_note: No standing rule on this platform names "an object literal used as a membership set inherits Object.prototype, so an inherited name indexes truthy". Recorded as not-citable for the second time in one day, deliberately: the first record (the SAIRNroofing instance) noted it as a candidate for a new rule, and finding the same shape at 48 sites within hours is the evidence that it should be one rather than a note on two records.
records.phase_note: Injected at design: the literal form is the convention the platform adopted at its first auth build and copied to every app after. It is not a coding slip -- the literal is correct-looking and matches every neighbour -- which is why it survived 19 files and is recorded as a design phase rather than an implementation one.

contributing_factors.factor: A JS object literal used as a membership set inherits every key on Object.prototype, and the platform expressed EVERY role gate that way -- 48 literals across 19 files. Each set was correct about every name it meant to accept and silent about the nine it never considered.
contributing_factors.action: All 48 now go through roleSet() in api/_lib/auth.js, which takes the literal and returns a null-prototype copy. ROLES_BY_APP and AUTH_TABLE_BY_APP too -- ROLES_BY_APP is indexed by payload.app inside verifySessionToken, where a plain literal made ROLES_BY_APP['constructor'] a truthy FUNCTION that then threw on .indexOf.

contributing_factors.factor: All 48 were inert for ONE distant reason: verifySessionToken() re-validates payload.role against ROLES_BY_APP on every verification. Nothing at any of the 48 gates said it depended on that, and nothing at verifySessionToken said it was load-bearing for them. A single point whose narrowing would open 48 gates at once.
contributing_factors.action: Each gate now refuses an inherited name on its own, so the central check is defence in depth rather than the only defence. The dependency is written down at api/_lib/auth.js where roleSet is defined, and the count of what depends on it is stated.

contributing_factors.factor: The finding as reported named NINE files. The real population is 48 literals in 19 files. The nine came from grepping two identifier names; the platform also uses AUTHENTICATED_ROLES, ALERT_ROLES, PRESCRIBER_ROLES, AI_COC_REVIEW_ROLES, FINANCIAL_ROLES and 25 function-local maps inside api/sd-data.js that no name-based grep would reach.
contributing_factors.action: The population is now derived by a SOURCE scan over git ls-files rather than by identifier name, and that scan is an arm of tests/role_maps_have_no_prototype.js with a non-zero-population control so it cannot report clean by having stopped matching.

contributing_factors.factor: Nothing on this platform could see the shape. It is invisible by construction: a plain literal role map reads correctly, matches eighteen other apps, and fails only on names nobody writes.
contributing_factors.action: tests/role_maps_have_no_prototype.js uses two structurally different methods -- a source scan (the only way to see the 25 function-local maps, which are never exported) and a runtime prototype check on the exported maps (the only way to catch one built correctly and mutated after) -- each with its own negative control. Registered in the push gate's GUARD_TESTS so it blocks rather than reports.

contributing_factors.factor: Eight sabotage controls copy a working-tree api/ file into a worktree at HEAD and did not copy its shared dependency, so every one went red AT THE BASELINE the moment sd-data.js started calling a helper from api/_lib/auth.js. An unstaged DEPENDENCY of a staged file is the same gap as an unstaged file and nothing named it as a class.
contributing_factors.action: api/_lib/auth.js added to the stage list of all eight, each with the reason written at the line. The harness diagnosed it by name in its own output, which is why it took minutes rather than a session -- the mechanism worked; what was missing was the class having a name.

records.recurrence_open: The actions close every role membership set currently in api/ and add a blocking guard against a new one. They do NOT close: (1) role maps expressed some other way -- an array read with .indexOf is safe and was counted and skipped, but a Set, a Map, or a switch would be outside both methods; (2) the same prototype-inheritance shape anywhere outside a role gate -- any object literal used as a lookup table keyed by caller-influenced data has it, and nothing counts those; (3) the client-side halves in the *.html files, which were not scanned at all; (4) the general question of what else, besides these role gates, silently depends on verifySessionToken's vocabulary check -- that dependency was discovered by reading, and nothing enumerates it.

records.subject: fix(security): the undecryptable-ciphertext logs named the wrong secret, and now name exactly one
records.summary: Both undecryptable-ciphertext diagnostics named the wrong secret. api/law-auth.js (attorney MFA/TOTP secret) said "tampered, or SD_AUTH_SECRET was rotated" and api/sc-eligibility.js (stored Stedi API key) said "SD_AUTH_SECRET rotated?". True when written; false since 509a04f6 split the encryption duty out on 2026-09-17, after which a `v2.` ciphertext is AES-keyed on sha256(SD_ENCRYPTION_KEY) and fails for a reason SD_AUTH_SECRET has nothing to do with. These are the first lines an incident responder reads -- docs/2026-09-24-sd-encryption-key-revoke.md routes them straight here -- so the cost lands entirely during an incident, on somebody already under time pressure, pointing at a variable whose rotation would not have caused what they are looking at. Fixed by deriving rather than by naming both candidates: each site reads the `v2.` prefix off the stored value, the same discriminator decryptSecret() branches on, and names the one key that wrote that ciphertext. No behaviour change -- same 500 MFA_UNAVAILABLE and 503 CREDENTIAL_UNREADABLE, same client payloads; only the server log differs.

injection.subject: feat(auth): split the encryption duty, add key rotation, and scope signing per app

records.citation_note: 2.3 is cited with a stretch, and the stretch is the reason for this note. Its shape fits exactly -- a stated fact carries a tense, and goes stale when the world it describes changes rather than when anybody edits it -- but 2.3 is written about STANDING DOCUMENTS, and these two facts live in a comment and a console.error inside shipped source. Nothing in Part 1 or Part 2 covers a fact asserted in code that is read only by a human, and only during an incident. Cited as arguable rather than recorded not-citable, because the family is right and only the scope is being widened: a source comment that states which env var is at fault is a standing document with a smaller audience and no review cadence at all.

contributing_factors.factor: THE KEY NAME WAS A LITERAL IN THE MESSAGE, not derived from anything. Both sites hardcoded 'SD_AUTH_SECRET' in a comment and a console.error at a point where the code already had the stored ciphertext in hand -- the one value that actually answers which key wrote it. A message stating a fact it does not read cannot stay true across a change to that fact.
contributing_factors.action: Each site now reads the `v2.` prefix off the stored value -- the same discriminator decryptSecret() itself branches on -- and names the single key that wrote that ciphertext. The message is now derived from the same source as the behaviour, so the two cannot disagree again.

contributing_factors.factor: THE 2026-09-17 SPLIT SWEPT BEHAVIOUR AND NOT PROSE. 509a04f6 changed which key decrypts and added the branch that decides, but the sweep stopped at code that ACTS on the key; the two call sites whose operator-facing text NAMED the key were left, and both still read as correct English about a system that had changed underneath them.
contributing_factors.note: No sweep tool was added here. The general form -- 'a message names an env var that a later change re-assigned' -- needs to know which key a code path actually uses, which is the hard half. The narrow form (an env-var literal inside a string or comment within a few lines of a decryptSecret() call) is cheap and buildable, and is recorded as a candidate rather than half-built inside a fix commit that declared two source files.

contributing_factors.factor: NOTHING ASSERTS ON OPERATOR-FACING LOG TEXT. api/_lib/auth.test.js covers the format choice and key selection thoroughly -- v2 vs legacy, rotation, unset key -- so the split was well tested in exactly the dimension that went stale, and every one of those tests stayed green while both diagnostics pointed at the wrong variable. Log strings are read only by a human during an incident, which is the worst moment to discover they are wrong.
contributing_factors.note: Pinning these two strings in a test would freeze the wording, not the truth of it: a test asserting the message says SD_AUTH_SECRET is exactly what the old text would have passed. What would actually bite is asserting the NAMED KEY MATCHES THE STORED FORMAT, which is the derivation this fix introduced -- so the fix removes the class rather than the test covering it.

records.recurrence_open: THE CLASS IS NOT CLOSED, only these two instances. Nothing stops the next operator-facing message from stating a fact it does not read, and the 2026-09-17 split is not the last time a duty will move between env vars. Specifically still open: (1) no inventory exists of messages that NAME an env var, so the blast radius of the next such split is unknown -- a grep across api/ for env-var literals inside strings and comments would produce it and has not been run; (2) legacy ciphertexts are still keyed on SD_AUTH_SECRET, so both branches of the new message are live and WHICH ROWS ARE STILL LEGACY has never been measured (the revoke doc says the same, and the select is still unrun); (3) the fix is verified by reading and by the surrounding suites, NOT by driving either path -- no test decrypts a v2 value with the wrong key and reads the log line, so the derivation is argued correct rather than observed correct.

records.subject: fix(controls): the rebase control was guarded all along, and a register count was counting itself
records.summary: Two measurement defects, each of which made a checker report the wrong thing about itself. (1) tools/sabotage_control_check.py reported tests/rebase_resolve_merge_control.py as UNGUARDED while that control carried a guard STRONGER than any spelling the detector knew: it tells a STALE ANCHOR apart from a NO-OP MUTATION, reports both, and exits 1 on either. The control guards tools/sairn_rebase_resolve.py, which every clone on this machine uses to merge docs/tier-a-reviews.json. This is the SIXTH time this detector has under-credited a well-written control, which inverts the signal it exists to give -- a probe that did the harder thing scoring worse than one that did the easy thing. The fix is the detector, not the probe: adding a decorative assert to satisfy a regex would be the inversion itself. (2) docs/CRITICALITY-TIERS.md said "N rows are marked CONFIDENTIALITY NOT YET INDIVIDUALLY READ" and instructed the reader to re-derive the figure with an unanchored `grep -c`, so the prose that REPORTS the count matched too and the prescribed re-derivation returned one too many EVERY TIME ANYBODY RAN IT. A SELF-COUNTING NUMBER IS WORSE THAN A STALE ONE: a stale number is wrong until somebody checks, and this one was wrong including when they did, because the instruction to check was what reproduced the error. It had also drifted on the other axis -- it read nine against an actual seven -- so correcting only the command would have left a wrong figure behind a right method.

injection.unknown_reason: Neither has an injection commit. The detector's vocabulary never covered the state-label spelling, and the grep command has counted its own sentence since the sentence was written.

records.citation_note: PR 1.11's subject is a check that could not run being folded into a pass. Both halves here are the mirror image: a control that DID run and was reported as absent, and a count whose prescribed re-derivation reproduced its own error. Same family -- a measurement that cannot be trusted to say what it measured -- read in the other direction, and cited rather than filed not-citable because the underlying principle is the same one.
records.phase_note: Neither was introduced in a phase. Both are omissions present from the first version of their subject.
records.factors_unknown_reason: Not yet worked through independently. The commit names them: a detector whose vocabulary is a list that only grows when somebody notices a miss, and a re-derivation instruction that is inside the thing it derives.

It says no artefact lost a genuine suite TODAY; it does not say the colon rule is the right rule -- driven separately, a set literal, a list, a tuple, a dict VALUE and a comment naming the artefact all still read as coverage, and the one file that motivated the fix is a dict only because its entries carry reason strings.
